speakeroldname: Mr. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a matter of
privilege I wish to call attention to a statement which I made on the budget debate, and which has been the subject of some adverse criticism and also of some very gross misrepresentation. In opening that debate I spoke as follows:
I notice that on the very evening on which the Minister of Finance made his budget speech, another gentleman, who is very prominent indeed or who wishes to be so, in the public life of this country, made a speech in the city ot Montreal in which he claimed to himself and one or two of his associates the full responsibility, and corresponding gratitude ot the public, for all the advantageous results which the Minister of Finance had noted. I do not know and I cannot judge from personal knowledge of the capacity of Sir Henry Thornton as an administrator of the railways of this country, but apparently he thinks that the Prime Minister, the Finance minister and the Minister of Railways are mere lunary satellites who become known to the public only when they stand in the reflected light of his great sun or star. But in this house we must look to the ministers of the government, who have assumed the responsibility of the administration of public affairs in Canada for a statement and explanation of their conduct in the administration of their respective offices, and I think the government and parliament and the people of this country would be better satisfied if Sir Henry Thornton would not so often obtrude himself into matters of which he has only a partial knowledge and no experience whatever.
Forty years ago I sat for some years as a member of the Press Gallery of this house, and therefore I appreciate the onerous duties and responsibilities of correspondents who sit in that gallery, upon whom the public rely for a fair statement of the proceedings of this house. So far as my experience goes, in the majority of cases, the fairness and accuracy with which these proceedings are reported does credit to the impartiality and competency of members of the press who sit in the gallery. But I find that the Ottawa correspondent of the London Advertiser, referring to the words which I have just quoted, sent the following report to his paper:
The outstanding feature of the _ speech delivered in the House of Commons this afternoon by C. H. Cahan, financial critic of the Conservative party, was a biting attack on the Canadian National Railw'ays and Sir Henry Thornton, the president of the government-owned system.
Hear, hear.

I remark this to the "hear, hears" of hon. gentlemen opposite, that there is not one statement in that entire speech which reflects discreditably upon either the national railways of Canada or upon the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning), who assumes the responsibility in this house for the administration thereof. Further, the correspondent of the London Advertiser proceeds:
Mr. Cahan was the official spokesman of the Conservative party, and presumably he uttered the opinions of the party as a whole when he attacked the national railways.
I think that is an unfair report of the proceedings of this house, and discreditable to the press representative who sent it to his paper, the London Advertiser. I notice also that the Ottawa Journal in dealing with these matters makes the suggestion to members on this side of the house that they should always keep quiet when they are likely to make statements which could possibly be misrepresented by the press correspondents of the house.
If that were carried out, Mr. Speaker, I am afraid the opposition would be entirely failing in the duties which it owes to parliament and to the public.
I would suggest to the right hon. the leader of the house (Mr. Mackenzie King), who in similar matters has had occasion to complain, that some measures should be taken to prevent utter misrepresentations of this character. It is well understood that the press correspondents are in the gallery only as a privilege which is due to the tolerance of this house, and unless we can have a fairer presentation of the proceedings to the public, if will be not only prejudicial to the house, as a house, but it will necessitate, I think, some measures being taken to prevent such misrepresentations being sent broadcast throughout the country.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. Speaking yesterday in the budget debate I said, as reported at page 702 of Hansard:
The third year of that parliament the budget was brought down embodying substantial reductions on farm machinery and other lines, and that budget received the support of the Progressives.

Half of the Progressives voted against it.
I have taken the trouble to look up the records of the house as recorded in Hansard, and I find that only one Progressive voted against that budget.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The year of the diamond jubilee of this confederation will pass into history as one of the most favourable and prosperous in all our national life. As a consequence, the annual budget, as announced by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), in many respects displays a creditable financial record, with years of the most careful administration.
Why should his message not be optimistic? -with evidence of prosperity on every hand, with three successive good harvests behind us, with prices of cereals as well as live stock and live stock products at least fairly satisfactory, which has placed agriculture in such a situation as to be able at least to reflect good times upon almost every class and industry in the land, I might add, on almost all but its own.
This condition, together with a greater mineral production, a further increase of forestry products, more particularly the newsprint industry, has so strengthened our industrial and manufacturing life, that, no matter whether they depend on the farm, the forest or the mines for their raw material, they appear to be fully assured of a sufficiency thereof, and a satisfactory market for their product. With such conditions abounding, those engaged in almost every field of national endeavour, outside of the farm, seem more than ever convinced that Canada has now entered upon the most wonderful development in our history. That being so, is it not the first duty of the government to see to it that as far as humanly possible every phase of our national and productive life shall receive even-handed justice in their means and cost of production, thus enabling and compelling every line of effort to rely upon themselves and upon the ingenuity of their own resources, rather than upon government favours, for material success in their business. That cannot be done in a day or in a twelve-month. It takes time to effect a satisfactory readjustment.
With regard to the sub-amendment which has just been proposed, I must confess that since I have had the honour of a seat in this house I have been at a loss to conceive any good reason why my hon. friends should persist in segregating themselves in the southeast corner of the chamber. After listening to their latest declaration I am more than ever surprised at the unexplainable attitude which they assume. The sub-amendment shows clearly that the difference between them and us on this side is one merely of degree and not of principle, and I am sorry indeed to find that my good friend the hon-

The Budget-Mr. McMillan
member for East Lambton (Mr. Fansher) has placed himself in such a position. If my hon. friends would only drop local, sectional considerations-

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Do you call that local?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
[DOT]-and view the situation from a national standpoint, there is not one syllable in the sub-amendment which should prevent them from standing with us and manifesting that broad-minded spirit of compromise which is so necessary to progress.
To the altogether admirable hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail), allow me to say in this special year when she seems quite unable to make the necessary approaches to any one of the three bachelor leaders in this house, I extend an invitation to come across to us, and we will be pleased to show her the most desirable pathway that leads to the promised land.
Possibly before I get through I may give my hon. friends even stronger reasons for a difference with the government, but such a difference expressed by resolution would prove fatal to the national welfare. I would advise my hon. friends, and even plead with them, to realize that it is not what any great leader thinks ought to be done that it is always wise to attempt at the moment, but it is rather what step in advance can be taken and at the same time carrying your countrymen with you. That is the great secret of progress in a true democracy.
It is also gratifying to notice that the tariff advisory board is getting after its work in earnest. In many cases the facts elicited are indeed illuminating. They clearly reveal the information, well known to every student of tariff matters, that the present Canadian customs tariff is a structure whose revision in many particulars is long overdue. A number of applications have been received from those enjoying a protection of 30 per cent and over, who say they are selling their goods at the level of world market prices and taking no advantage of the tariff. If that is so, why the need of such protection? And yet the ghosts these men see are weird beyond belief. The manufacturers of enamelware, for instance, put in their story the fear of competition from Japan, and yet the total value of imports of enamelware from Japan in five years was only $214. In one of those years we actually imported six dollars' worth of enamelware from Japan. This constant fear of competition from countries of cheap labour is childish. No nation will ever become a great commercial nation without rich and varied mineral and other resources. Providence has blessed Canada with great natural wealth; we ought to become one of the greatest trading nations in the world, and the desire of the government and the people should be gradually to scale down all needless trade barriers and go forth to meet the open competition of the world. We watch our manufacturers as they push the sale of their products in the world's markets, and we are proud of them; we see them as they go out to conquer and, as they are conquering abroad. Why do they stand and shiver at the thought of meeting foreign competition at home? They are willing to fly their commercial flags in the markets of the world; why allow them to hang at half-mast in Canada? Why should our Canadian consumers be compelled to bear the additional burden? Why not get down gradually to a strictly revenue tariff?
From the cradle to the grave we have had preached to us, through the medium of this customs tariff, the gospel of our inferiority. Talk about an inferiority complex; the very thought of the thing is humiliating. It reminds me of the attitude of the British boot and shoe manufacturers about 1907 or 1908, when they appealed to the British government for protection against the American boot and shoe trade, saying there was such an inrush of American goods that they already had established American branch stores and were rapidly driving the British manufacturers of boots and shoes out of their own home market. Of course the British government gave to those people the only answer a British government could give, that it would never do to burden the whole British people to benefit a few boot and shoe makers. This compelled those manufacturers to turn their attention in another direction, so they renovated their dilapidated plants and brought them up to date. They also remodelled the styles of their footwear and brought them up to date, and what was the result? In less than three years they had driven almost every American boot and shoe out of the British market, and even the American branch shops were selling British made goods. Even before the war they began to successfully invade the Canadian and American markets with British made goods. Such would no doubt be the effect of a well-considered, substantial reduction of the Canadian customs tariff. It has been so in the past. It was eminently so in the case of the automobile tariff reduction, in the face of the great hue and cry which closed the Oshawa shops for the moment and sent a great deputation to Ottawa, many of whom got lost in Hull simply because they did not seem to know whether they were walking on terra firma or in the moon.

The Budget-Mr. McMillan
This customs tariff in its application has been in many ways a species of the most glaring economic injustice. Ever since my boyhood days it has hung like a millstone around the necks of a great majority of our people, and more particularly the agricultural and labouring classes. Surely it is a thousand times more important to the welfare of Canada that we should have a healthy and prosperous agriculture than that any other industry should be able through the medium of a high tariff to wring undue prices from the consuming public. More than that, we find many applications before the board even from manufacturers seeking a reduction of tariff on their raw material. They admit that tariffs add to their costs; scores of them have asked relief on their necessary requirements, and we can readily see that relief to manufacturers may also mean relief to consumers.
You may ask whether agriculture is not now prosperous. The answer is that agriculture is not as prosperous as it ought to be, nor as prosperous as it might easily be made. While some farmers do not make the effort which they might make, yet with the present economic handicaps and the clamour for an eight hour day, a half holiday in the middle of the week, and two or three weeks holidays in the middle of the summer which .those in other lines of life are getting,, no farmer can make a success on the farm, and those who are making it go are the ones who toil from sun to sun, and whose women's work is never done. The man and bis good wife who pledge themselves to each other for life and decide to make their livelihood by dairying and allied lines are entitled to every just consideration by the government. I have sat in the homes of those who are recognized as our most successful farmers, and have discussed the situation with those high-minded wives and mothers, who with the keenest maternal feeling have recounted the experiences of their life's toil, saying that it seemed not so bad when they were young and strong but was now almost unbearable. They have repeatedl}'- appealed to me to know if I really thought they should advise their sons and daughters to stick to the farm and repeat their own experiences in life. Yet, Sir, the lasting wrelfare of this country depends upon the principles that underlie agriculture. What do we see to-day? All over this country agriculture is losing the best and brainiest youths from our rural homes, and it is becoming impossible to replace them with suitable help. We talk about the problems of government. Sir, the greatest problem before this country to-day is the problem of keeping 
our own people on the farm, not of keeping them in Canada. We hear much from our friends opposite of the trek to the United States. Such remarks are very unpatriotic and largely beside the truth. The greatest trek in our history was between 1881 and 1891 when the national policy of protection was in the very height of its glory.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is pretty high still, is it not?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As I say, this is a
problem which stares us in the face. No one seems to want to discuss it but the time has come when the people of this country, and more particularly their representatives in this house, ought to discuss this problem and find a remedy for it. This is a national situation. If we look upon ourselves merely as the creatures of a day, what difference does it need to make to us if conditions are never any better? It will only be a few years until we too are off the scene. If we are here for any good purpose we are here for the welfare of posterity, and we should endeavour to make the conditions under which they will live better than the conditions which we enjoy to-day.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Your place is over here.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You people should come to this side. Sitting where you are now you are only holding back the wheels of progress, whereas if .you took your places here you would be able to help them on. As I say, this is a problem which is staring us in the face and we must grappLe with it. The facts are that throughout this Dominion agriculture is losing the best and the brainiest young folks from our rural homes, and it cannot lose them and prosper. It is far from my view of life that every youth born on the farm should1 remain there. I have discussed this matter with scores of our brightest young men, and they tell me the only reason why they are directing their course elsewhere is because they cannot see a sufficient margin of profit easily obtained on the home farm. That has been the case for years. It was the case when a big deputation of farmers waited on the Laurier government in 1910, but it is greatly aggravated to-day. In looking over the proceedings of that deputation the other day I find I then made the following observation :
The farmers are willing to meet any legitimate competition in the labour market of the country. He does not wish to underpay the workmen. His desire is to remunerate them well. But when he is compelled to face a statutory tariff provision which takes from him

The Budget-Mr. McMillan
annually a margin of millions, and those millions are employed in competing with him on his own home labour, he cannot stand an unjust competition such as that.
Those conditions are greatly intensified today. You may ask: Where are those millions of which you speak, obtained by our tariff beneficiaries with which they are able to compete for our agricultural labour? In a moment or two I will give you one concrete instance, but the reply broadly is that other lines of industry are able to obtain their necessary requirements either free or at the lowest possible rates of duty. Why should the agriculturists be deprived of the same privilege? Is the welfare of agriculture a matter of such secondary consideration in this country that it should be required to take a subordinate position?

speechtext:
Now, Sir, I say that
agriculture is largely a domestic industry. But it is far more than that. It is the one great uncontaminated seed-bed of our population. In this respect there is no other situation in life to compare with it. Should that not count for something in the social welfare? As I say, farming is largely a domestic industry. Consider its requirements! Take agricultural implements, machinery, building materials, food, clothing and other household requirements. These comprise over 60 per cent of the needs of our agricultural life. Take the first of these-agricultural implements. They have not a high duty, only from 6 to 10 per cent. But I ask this question:
Is it of more importance to the welfare of this country that the implement makers should be given a preference and allowed to make money and grow wealthy than that agriculture should so prosper that it would present a good living and comfortable homes to the millions for which it is looking? Sir, the question carries its own answer. We do not ask a preference, but if there is a preference going, agriculture should have that preference, and in no case should agriculture be discriminated against. Agriculture employs one-third of our gainfully employed population. Therefore it follows that a successful agriculture means a prosperous nation. Moreover, it is the first principle in this tariff that those manufactured goods which are exported to foreign countries are given a drawback equal to from 60 to 99 per cent of the duty on the raw material used. That provision gives to the residents of other countries our own goods cheaper than our own people can get them. Where is agriculture allowed any such equivalent? The agricultural industry is by far the greatest exporting agency we have got. Where is it allowed any drawback on its products exported? Absolutely none. The only way by which you can allow any such compensating advantage is to give to agriculture its necessary requirements free. And implements are only one of the hundred and one other things in the line of machinery which the farmer requires which all carry a tariff burden of from 20 to 35 per cent.
Turn to another line. Take paint. One would imagine the rate on paint would be low. Paint is a prime necessity in national economy. It is the rawest of raw materials. It enters or should enter into the construction of almost every building in the land. Yet the duty on white-lead ground in oil, which is the real basis of paints, is 37i per cent among the highest of all ad valorem duties in the tariff schedule. One would think the manufacturers would stand hand in hand with the Consumers League in removing such anomalies. But they seem to fear the slightest touch upon that frail structure of protection.

speechtext: What about the government?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My hon. friend talks about the government. That talk is in line with their amendment. They want everything done to-day, and they will never get any further when they adopt that attitude.

speechtext:
We want
something done.
The Budget-Mr. McMillan

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It will be only a few years before my hon. friend will be no longer in the sun but will be in the shade. Let me say that protection as applied to trade and industry is a misnomer. Prevention is the proper term. Perhaps that is the reason why our hon. friends across the way dropped the word "protection" entirely at the Winnipeg convention, but every argument which is presented has that principle in ambush behind the shade.
Let us consider the cotton industry. That has already been placed before the house, but for the purpose of my argument I am going to place it again. The protection in Canada on manufactured cotton goods under the general tariff is not far from thirty per cent, and is sometimes more. Every time a Canadian workman buys a piece of cotton cloth in Canada he pays an exorbitant price as compared with the world price of those goods. Apparently, however, the cotton lords do not appear to think so. Their viewpoint was very clearly stated before the tariff board by that eminent Montreal lawyer, Mr. Aime Geoffrion, when he said in speaking of wages as a factor in the cost of production:
As a matter of fact we deny the principle involved in the suggestion, if wages are to be considered, everything spent in Canada should be considered. In other words, all that is a factor. In deciding what should be the measure of protection, it can only be on the suggestion that there is money spent in Canada by which the consumer benefits. So, in that way, there is no distinction made between wages and salaries, purchases from local merchants, and any other expenditure in Canada.
In other words, the contention is that the people of Canada, the consumers, should provide the manufacturer of cotton goods with everything except his raw cotton. There is not other way we can do this than by paying an exorbitant price for our cotton goods. That is what we are doing now, and that we are doing it to the full limit of the tariff there is ample reason to believe. At the recent cotton hearing, the chairman pointed out that there was clear evidence that the manu-. facturers were in some cases taking full advantage of the tariff, and yet, according to their story, it is -absolutely impossible for them to survive. Have they survived? Yes. Is the Canadian Cottons, Limited, doing well? This is their financial statement as summarized in the Financial Times:
The balance sheet of Canadian Cottons, as of March 31, 1927, shows a surplus of $2,737,563 equivalent to over $100 a share on the 27,155 shares of common stock. In addition there is shown among their liabilities an item of $600,000 for special replacement reserve, despite a generous reserve for depreciation. If this 
sum was added to the surplus, the latter would be shown to be equal to $123 a share on the common stock.
Yet they would lead us to believe that they are going broke.
Let us consider the Dominion Textiles, Limited, the story of which company records some of the most remarkable adventures in Canadian financial and industrial history. The present owners paid $500,000 for stock with a par value of $5,000,000. Year after year they paid dividends on its par value. Then as the stock went up in price they gave to every holder of two shares the right to purchase an additional share at par when the stock was selling far above par. A year ago they split the stock in three; that is, every shareholder got three shares for one, and today that stock sells on the market for $130 a share. The company has a capitalized valuation of $29,000,000, and in all the yeais since it was formed only $3,000,000 has been paid for the stock. If we measure the profits paid to-day against the actual amount of cash paid by the original owners, we find the actual earnings of Dominion Textiles, Limited, to be in excess of 220 per cent. But that is not all. How fared this company in the hour of the nation's peril when it was expected that every citizen and more particularly every wealthy corporation should be doing everything possible to strengthen the allied cause? At page 362 of the evidence in the report of the special committee on the cost of living which sat in 1919, the then president admitted that the company earned a dividend of about 291 per cent. This is only one line of industry which has been considered and reported upon by the tariff advisory board, but the information is startling. Is it not time that a halt was being called on behalf of the consuming public of Canada to this kind of thing? In these lines of goods it would pay the Canadian consumer well to keep the extra margin which these cotton duties compel him to pay, with that margin pension every wage earner in those factories to the full extent of the wages they receive and let them go idle all the year, and they w-ould still have a good surplus left.
In the case of agriculture employing one-third of our gainfully employed population, it follows that those engaged therein must bear a large part of that burden. Let us turn the tables for a moment or, as a schoolboy would say, "Turn about is fair play." Surely no one will contend that the cotton industry is of more importance than agriculture. How would it be if we now suggest paying the wage bill of those employed in agriculture, let alone an annual dividend of 291 per cent

The Budget-Mr. Clark
of the cash price of the land? Would not that proposition, if carried into effect, "Make Farmer John a smile put on?" Why, the problem would be solved. You could not keep the people off the land.
I conclude by asking the same question which I put earlier in my remarks: Is it not a thousand times more important to the welfare of Canada that agriculture should be so prosperous that it would present a good living and comfortable homes to the millions for whom we are looking, than that any of these other industries should be able to grow wealthy at the expense of agriculture and the general consuming public? We have abundant economic proof that agriculture is not as prosperous as it ought to be? We are all agreed that at the moment we have, generally speaking, prosperous times in this country. Apart from the capital now in Canada seeking investment, foreign capital is rushing in by the hundreds and millions. Where is it being invested? We have just passed the new year, and we have noticed writers galore expatiating on the good times the country is enjoying and the fine opportunities for the investment of capital. Have you noticed anyone saying that capital, in large amounts is rushing in for profitable investment in our rich agricultural lands, the finest natural asset this country possesses. Yet that is where we all agree that more of our people ought to be and, moreover, if the people could see a sufficient margin easily obtainable, that is where they would be. You could not keep them off the farms; they would be falling over each other to get on the land.
If we are desirous of seeing more of our people on the land, why stand shivering on the brink of doing what ought to be done? The vital importance of successful agriculture is such that farming is far more than an industry. The significance of agriculture in the life of this nation is far deeper than this. Employing as it does about one-third of our gainfully employed population, it touches something really vital and fundamental in our national existence. It involves the continued national prosperity, the economic welfare, the racial character, and the social progress of the Canadian people. We must as a people determine, and it is the duty of this house as the servants of the people to determine, deliberately and wisely the role we wish to have agriculture play in our national economic life. Now is the time to decide. You cannot do this kind of thing during periods of dull times. You can do it only when times are prosperous and trade is buoyant. The golden opportunity has come, and it is the bounden duty of this government, now when it has begun the work,
to take opportunity by the hand and go to it deliberately and wisely. If we wish to see agriculture thrive and prosper and present a good living and comfortable homes to the millions for whom we are looking, then free it from its present unjust economic restrictions. If this is not done, it may well be said that what is badly needed, not only throughout this country but in this house, is such a readjustment of national ideas as will place agriculture and its claims to the best intelligence and the highest skill of our people in the very forefront of national thought. When that reawakening is sufficiently emphatic-and God speed the day of such an awakening, that it may come ere the progeny of the noblest pioneers who ever settled any country have all deserted the farms-there will then be no more hastening away from the farm, but rather such a just conception of agriculture as our main resource and our most dignified and independent vocation as will attract to its just aim in the improvement of methods^ the increase of yields, and in the clearing away of the unjust restrictions which lie across its path, the wisdom and the science and the willing hands of millions, who may then obtain a just remuneration for their labour, and at the same time hand on to posterity an unimpaired inheritance.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, though my remarks will be critical in their nature, I do not want it thought that I am not grateful to Providence for the bountiful crops w'hich we have had during the past few years, nor that I am not extremely grateful for the influx of capital into this country as well as for the use of Canadian capital in developing our mines and our natural resources, nor that I am ungrateful also for the great energy displayed by our people in the development of those resources. I do not, however, admit that in the development of those resources this government has had any hand.	_
I cannot hope to analyze in detail the budget brought down by the Minister of Finance, but I must take note of a few of its salient features.	_
First of all, I would like to point to the method by which the Minister of Finance has arrived at his surplus. I see in the public accounts a certified statement foy a firm of chartered accountants that the net debt of the Dominion does not include the issues of the Canadian National Railways guaranteed by this government. I find that those guaranteed issues have, since the present Minister of Finance took office, amounted to $200,000,000. True, $34,000,000 was in the nature of the

The Budget-Mr. Clark
refunding of an indebtedness due by the Grand Trunk Pacific, which was not previously guaranteed by this country, and another $20,000,000 was for refunding of issues which were guaranteed; so that allowing $54,000,000 for refunding, there has been added to the indebtedness of this country by guarantees the sum of approximately $146,000,000.
Now the Minister of Finance over the same period claims a reduction in the net debt of the country of $105,000,000. Actually if those guarantees were added to the net debt of the country, as they should have been, we would find that there has been over the period during which the Minister of Finance has held office a deficit of some $45,000,000 to $50,000,000. which is not shown in the statement presented by the Minister of Finance this year or in any year since he took office.
I find also that since 1925 there appears to have been a reckless tendency on the part of this government to increase its expenditures. The public accounts disclose that for 1925 our total expenditures amounted to some $339,900,000. That sum increased in 1928, estimated, to $366,000,000, and taking the estimates for the current fiscal year, which are now before the house we find that that amount is still further increased to $373,796,000. If you allow $12,000,000 for supplementary estimates, a fair average, we find that the total expenditure for 1928-29 will be approximately $385,796,000-a total increase since 1925 in this country's expenditure of approximately $50,000,000. I do not think that members of this house can emphasize too strongly this fact, that there has been an increase of $50,000,000 in the country's expenditure in those four short years. And what have we to show for that increase?
I have heard it observed by speakers on the opposite side of the house that this is the people's budget. I suppose that we can assume that the farmers of this country form part of the people, yet what do we find in this budget that is of value to the farmers? I have read and reread this budget, and I have at last found that the Minister of Finance did not forget the farmers. I find an item which does relate to the farmers and which is supposed to benefit that great class, for whom the Minister of Finance must have very strong feelings because the item is the first one in the new schedules, reading:
Small onion plants grown from seeds and imported for bona fide transplanting or propagation purposes.
These are put on the free list, and that is the one and only item in this budget wdiich relates to the farmers of this country or is supposed to benefit them. The only con-IMr. Clark.]
elusion to which I can come is that the Minister of Finance must be personally fond of onions, and I am wondering why he did not add pea soup.
I think we might also include among, the people of this country the employed classes. I find that the family budget to-day is as high as it was five years ago; I am not so sure that it is not higher, but at any rate there has been no reduction in the cost of living since this government took office. But worse than that. In the manufacturing industries of this country there were in 1910, 515,203 employees in industrial establishments. Taking it by five year periods, I find that in 1915 there were 514.883 employees, and in 1920 that number had risen to 609,586. In case it may be thought that I am taking a peak year, I will give the figure for 1917, in which year there were 621,694 employees in the factories of this country. In 1924. the last year for which the figures are available, we find that in the industrial establishments of this country there were 508,503 employees, or some seven thousand less than in the year 1910. I ask the government, Does that indicate progress? There is this reduction despite the fact that we have in this country a new and great industry, the automobile industry, and its allied industries, such as the rubber industry and other new industries, which did not exist in 1910. Obviously, since this government took office it has destroyed many of our industries. The best evidence of that is to be seen in the empty factories throughout the country. But there are the figures. I asked the Bureau of Statistics for them, and I went back and had them rechecked to make sure that they were given on a comparative basis.
Furthermore, my friends on the left and the Minister of Finance also have emphasized another point-reduction in taxation, brought about by this so-called "people's budget ", One of the big reductions we are told is in the income tax. I find that to-day the income tax affects only 116,000 of our people, or a little over one per cent of our total population, and they are the wealthy classes. Does that reduction in taxation indicate that this is a people's budget? Are the payers of income tax the common people that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe)-who, I presume, is now leading the government-was working to benefit when he assisted in bringing down these budget proposals? I see the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke)-not in his seat, but in the house; was he working for the common people when he put his imprimatur upon these budget proposals? How about the poor people who are affected by the sales

The Budget-Mr. Clark
tax? True, the sales tax is reduced by one point, but it is still at the level at which the government found it when they took office. Our people are in the same position in relation to the sales tax as they were when the Liberal party took office, and it is high time that the sales tax was wiped out if the government desires to benefit the common people. The other great reduction in taxation that is claimed by our friends opposite has to do with the business profits tax. Two years ago this tax stood at 9 per cent; last year it was reduced to 8.1 per cent, to-day it is still further reduced to 8 per cent. Now, what does that mean? It means simply this. A business which made a profit of $10,000 last year paid a tax of $810, as a result of the budget proposals that business will get the advantage this year of the great reduction of $10-it will have to pay only $800 on its $10,000 profit.
One of the most noteworthy statements made by the Minister of Finance in his budget is this:
The value of working for closer trade relations within the empire is surely apparent.
And he quotes these figures for the fiscal year 1927: our sales to the empire, $542,000000; our purchases $214,000,000-a balance in our favour of $328,000,000. I agree with the Minister of Finance that it is worth while working for closer trade relations within the empire. But it would be amusing were it not tragic to analyze the way in which he has proceeded to work for these closer trade relations. During the time he has been in control of the Finance department he has made eight trade treaties, six with foreign countries. As a result of those eight trade treaties he reduced our favourable trade balance in the calendar year 1927 by $23,000,000 compared with the figures for the calendar year 1926. This seems to me like a hand-out to foreign countries, but that apparently is the policy of the minister and the policy of the government. It looks like a foreign improvement policy, rather than an attempt at working for closer and better trade relations within the empire.
Let us take these eight trade treaties and deal with them in order. Two of them are with British dominions, Australia and New Zealand. Let me take Australia first. In the calendar year 1927 our exports were $2,300,000 in round figures, less than in the previous calendar year; our imports were $1,200,000 more-or a decreased favourable trade balance of over three and a half million dollars. New Zealand: our exports for the calendar year 1927 were nearly $3,700,000 less than in 1926; our imports were $2,000,000 more-a decrease in our favourable trade balance of $5,700,000. Belgium: for the calendar year 1927 our exports decreased $3,400,000; our imports increased $1,200,000-a decrease in our favourable trade balance of $4,600,000. France:	This is
really the most illuminating of all, because if we go back to the time when the treaty came into force we shall find that we had a favourable trade balance of $7,000,000. For the calendar year 1927 we have a favourable trade balance changed into an unfavourable trade balance of seven and a half million dollars. In other words, in the calendar year 1927 we decreased our exports by $3,500,000; we increased our imports by $4,000,000-or an increased unfavourable trade balance of $7,500,000. British West Indies: The same story. The favourable trade balance for the calendar year 1926 -of $715,000 is changed to an unfavourable trade balance of $1,500,000. Japan:	We decreased our favourable balance
by $8,668,000. With only two countries do we find that we have improved our trade- Italy and The Netherlands. With Italy we increased our favourable trade balance by $8,500,000. Let me point out to my friends to the left that that is represented mainly by the increase of $7,941,000 in our wheat exports for the calendar year 1927 as compared with 1926. That great increase was due to the failure of wheat shipments from Odessa. The same thing is true of The Netherlands. We increased our favourable trade balance by $660,000, but this is more than accounted for by the fact that we increased our wheat exports by $4,000,000, due again to the failure of wheat shipments from Odessa. The day is coming, I fear, when Russia will come back into the world's wheat markets. Only one thing is hindering the return of Russia into the wheat market of the world, and that is the lack of unity within that country, due to the fact that Russia is composed of more than two hundred races that cannot unite politically or economically. But should they ever be able to unite economically, think, Mr. Speaker, of the menace to this country in our foreign trade in wheat and other commodities.
But, sir, more serious than that, something which in my view transcends in importance every other problem that confronts Canada to-day, is the situation in regard to immigration. Here I challenge our Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to point to any other five-year period in the history of the Dominion when the emigration of Canadians

The Budget-Mr. Clark
to the United States or to any other country exceeded our immigration. Yet that is the situation in the period between the fiscal years March 31, 1922 and March 31, 1927. I have heard this sneered at by members on the other side, but according to the figures secured by myself from the Bureau of Statistics-	.

Then the minister is indulging in empty talk. ' These figures show that 591,121 persons, including Newfoundlanders, entered the United States as immigrants in a given period. AVe can secure figures in regard to Newfoundlanders only for the last two years, but they would indicate that about 2,000 Newfoundlanders go to the United States per annum. Allowing, say, 7,000 for the previous three years-I am quite prepared to allow 10,000 Newfoundlanders, but let us say 7,000. We find that 11,257 fewer people came into the country than went out. I suppose the Minister of Railways will say, "But think of the returning Canadians!" I have heard the Prime Minister and every other minister on the other side say the same thing. But I took the precaution to get these figures from the Immigration department and I am not afraid to give them; I do not mind giving them.
I would ask hon. gentlemen opposite, however, to recall that Canadians have been going to the United States since confederation, and while some of those may be among these returned Canadians they are not classed as immigrants. If they were once Canadians and they have come back they are not entered^ as immigrants, at least according to the information given me by the department. Last year, our Immigration department claims 42,078 came back from the United States. They are returning Canadians, and I fancy it would be very difficult to tell whether or not they are all Canadians who went to the United States as immigrants.
Now there was a time, only ten short years ago, when the blood of a Canadian was a matter of some consequence in this country. Canadians then took very much to heart,

the tragic fate of our 60,000 dead who were laid to rest in the battlefields of France and Flanders, not to mention 50,000 permanently injured. It was freely predicted then that Canada could not stand the strain on her manhood but under this government, according to the official statistics of the United States, we have suffered nearly 800,000 casualties; and if the truth were known, including the underground route we have lost at least a million to the United States. And practically all these casualties sacrificed to the United States were native-born Canadians. But the greater tragedy is that they are in the United States competing with this country.
How are we replacing these Canadians? I further challenge our Prime Minister to point to any speech he has made in this house- and I have searched Hansard-or to any speech he has made in the country, or to any act on the part of this government, wherein this problem has been grappled with in a fair-minded, broad, constructive manner. All I can find in Hansard are empty statements that Canadians are returning, together with suggestions to the effect that members on this side of the house are unpatriotic in bringing the question to the attention of the country. A\ ell, Mr. Speaker, if I am responsible for keeping one of these intending immigrants at home, I shall be content, providing I can influence the government to any extent in grappling with the question and endeavouring to keep our Canadians in this Dominion.
Let us see how this government has dealt with the question of replacing Canadians. I take the last fiscal year as an example; I presume that it must represent the policy of this government, though as a matter of fact no policy has been announced. However, I presume that these figures will indicate at least the desires of the government. The Minister of Railways laughs, as he usually does, but the fact is that last year was the one year since confederation when more foreigners entered this country than British and Americans combined. Is that something to Jaught at? Perhaps it is to the Minister of Railways, but to no other Canadian.

Now I will give a few of

I find that there were 4,863 Jewish, 3,466 Italians, 4,941 Magyars, 6,700 Poles, 10,061 Ruthenians, and so forth. I will not go through the whole list. I want to say at once that I am not reflecting upon these people; they are in all probability the most admirable of their race that can be found. I repeat, I am not reflecting upon them. I suggest, however, that if you mix, as are mixed in Russia, all the races of the world, you cannot expect that unity which we all desire. It cannot be achieved under such conditions; it would take generations to assimilate these people into anything like a united whole. That is why I refer to this aspect of the question. And now let me give a list of others who entered the country last year. There were Albanians, Austrians, Bohemians, Bulgarians, Creations, Czechs, Dalmatians, Esthonians, Finnish, Greeks, Italians, Jews, Jugo-Slavs, Letts, Lithuanians, Magyars, Maltese, Mexicans, Moravians, Poles, Portuguese, Rumanians, Russians, Ruthenians, Serbs, Slovaks, Spaniards, Turks, Arabians, Armenians, Chinese, Japanese, Negroes, Persians, and Syrians.
