Now, what is the irresistible conclusion to be drawn from these figures and from the exodus to the United States? There is only one conclusion, and that is the racial complexion of the Canadian people is changing, and changing at such an alarming rate that we cannot stand very many more years of it if we are to remain an Anglo-Saxon and French race. I wonder if this situation appeals to my hon. friends from Quebec; I do not think it does. I firmly believe that they appreciate the fact that the Anglo-Saxon has been the fairest, truest and most broad-minded friend the French have ever had, and I really believe in the heart of every French-Canadian is the desire that, apart from the French-Canadians themselves, the Anglo-Saxon shall be predominant. I do not think there are many in the province of Quebec, I doubt if there would be a handful, who would follow the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), who says that if we want to bring about secession in this country we should bring in the British as immigrants. No, Mr. Speaker, there are not many of that type, because it has been too lately proven on the battlefields of France that the British race is most versatile and adaptable and possesses the greatest power of endurance, much greater than that required by immigrants into this country. The British adapted themselves to circumstances previously unknown, and proved themselves to be the

The Budget-Mr. Clark

best on earth. Let me recall the statement made by Marshal Foch, who said that it was the "hammer blows of the British army" which won the war, or words to that effect. They are the men, Mr. Speaker, who, it is sometimes suggested, are not fit to be immigrants to this country. No man can convince fair minded Canadians that the average Britisher is not loyal to the empire, that he does not understand the principles of British fair play or that he is not three generations ahead of every other available immigrant in suitability as a prospective citizen of this country.
In addition to that, Mr. Speaker, when the Britisher comes here he stays with us. I recall the figures placed on Hansard two or three years ago by the member for Victoria (Mr. Tolmie), which have never been controverted and as to which there has been no suggestion of inaccuracy. Those figures covered the period from 1900 to 1921, and of the various races entering this country we find that 77 per cent of the American born left while 23 per cent remained; 52 per cent of the foreigners left and 48 per cent remained, while only 36 per cent of the British left and 64 per cent remained. Surely these facts indicate the suitability of the British immigration and that we can and should attempt to secure them.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I appeal to this government to adopt the policy of the Australian government. I appeal to our Prime Minister to forget his constitutional theories, and with all the sincerity in my soul I ask him to go to the next Imperial conference determined to take a leading part, and to sit down with the representatives of the British government and ascertain whether there is not something that can be done to bring about a much greater British immigration to this Dominion, and to all the British dominions, for that matter. Furthermore, I appeal to him to promote those trade relations to which the Minister of Finance referred, by every means, to see if we cannot band together this British empire into an economic entity which will set an example to the world at large.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very much interested in the statements made by the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Fansher) yesterday, more especially as he seemed to base most of his remarks on the Liberal platform of 1919. He stated that he stood by that platform, and as one of the Labour party who has perhaps been suspected of being somewhat more favourable to the Liberals than to the other party I felt that I was not quite so lonesome after the hon. gentleman laid 
the foundation for what he said on the Liberal platform of 1919. I am not ashamed to say that I do adhere to the Liberal policies. In fact my leader has on more than one occasion seen fit to introduce me to some of his friends in this peculiar phraseology of his:	Allow me to introduce to you
my Liberal-Labour friend, or what would be called in the old country a Lib-Lab. So that I propose to discuss this question this afternoon from a Liberal standpoint. I am not ashamed of Liberal policies, but I am ashamed of Liberal practices. During the years when I sat close to Doctor Clark, who was perhaps one of the ablest exponents of free trade and Liberalism that this country has ever seen, nothing was greater gall and wormwood to me, and to others in our district, than to have the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) come to our meetings and very truthfully tell us that for years and years the Liberal party had been urging the lowering of the tariff, but when they had the opportunity they only lowered it about one-tenth of one per cent on the whole. Last year I think I made the remark that in 1911 those who believed so strongly in protection had crucified Sir Wilfrid Laurier on the cross of protection. Today it is obvious that another crucifixion is taking place which is even more important, and that is the crucifixion of Liberal principles.
A great deal was said in the budget speech about our expenditures, and there were many references to the annual financial statement m regard to our prosperity. I am very glad to be able to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) upon his ability to meet those expenditures and still have a surplus. I am not going to attack the budget to-day along that particular line. I am critical not so much of the surplus on hand, but of the steps which are being taken to meet our obligations. That I think is the crux of the situation, and that is the point I intend to deal with in my address. There has been a great deal of attack upon the income tax. I have received protests against the income tax from the retailers' association, and others, and one of the salient arguments advanced was this: If the income tax were abolished we should be able to put more money into industry. That is quite true. If all taxes were abolished I am quite sure we should be aJble to put more money into industry. I should be very glad to see all my taxes abolished because I should be able to engage in business to a greater extent than I am able to at present. I do not, however, see that as any particular argument. We must get money

The Budget-Mr. Adshead
from somewhere to meet our obligations and the question is, where is that money to come from? It is upon the subject of this diminishing income tax, and the promise of still further reduction in that taxation, that I propose to make a few remarks, and I hope not to take forty minutes. Perhaps if we turn to what other countries are doing in this matter we may be able to form some idea as to where Canada stands. I hold here a statement made by an expert in financial affairs, to the following effect:
In England 45 per cent of the total revenue -an enormous sum-comes from inheritance and income taxes-including the super taxes. Sixty-four per cent of American tax revenues are from income tax-in Canada less than 14 per cent. The groans of those who bear this burden, much of it falling upon war profits, have melted the heart of the Minister of Finance. There is a 10 per cent reduction in income tax and, on balance, practically nothing in tariff reductions. There is also the definite warning that unless Liberalism asserts itself the income tax will disappear within a few years and wealth untaxed rule the roost. We have heard for a long period of time the contention that the tariff could not be lowered. We have been told that the necessities of the revenue prevented such action. We see now the hollowness of the argument. We have in the income tax a steady and unfailing source of revenue. Year after year it has been cut. In 1927 it brought to the government coffers over $48,000,000. It has proved itself in England and the United States the backbone of an efficient system of taxation. There is no justification for its reduction to-day. To reduce the income tax while the tariff remains as it is, is a budget decision which will meet with scant approval from forward looking people throughout Canada.
That is the opinion of an expert in taxation matters. However, I think we ought to go back to an earlier date than that of this statement. I took occasion the other day to read the addresses of those hon. gentlemen in the Liberal ranks who supported the income tax when it was inaugurated in 1917. I notice that Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the late Mr. Carvell, and Mr. A. K. Maclean, of Halifax, supported the proposal. I also note that you yourself, Mr. Speaker, made a very eloquent appeal in favour of the income tax on that memorable day, July 25, 1917. I propose to read to the house the opinions of Liberals upon the subject of income tax when that form of taxation was brought into force. On page 3767 of Hansard of 1917, I find the following remarks by Mr. Maclean:
One great value of this form of taxation will be that the taxpayer will take a greater interest in the expenditure of any money which he contributes directly to the public treasury. One of the evil effects of indirect taxation is that the taxpayer is apparently never fully seized of the fact that he is contributing anything in taxation to the public 50103-461
treasury. . . . It is in the interest of sound national finance that we should have in this country some form of income taxation, and I have no doubt that once we have embarked upon it, the judgment of the country will be that it should be continued for many years to come.
He went on and said that if the country feared that the income tax wohld impede immigration such a fear could be easily removed by lowering the rate of customs duty which was excessive. I maintain that that is exactly the position which we in this corner of the house take. That was the position of the old Liberal opposition, but it appears to me that the Liberals have forsaken that policy and are decreasing the income tax but not lowering the tariff. Then too, Mr. Carvell, at page 3770 of Hansard of the same year, said that the income tax had become an institution in Canada. He added:
I was glad the minister did not state he would abolish it at the close of the war. It will never be abolished, because the good sense of the people of Canada will see it is kept in effect for all time.
In spite of these declarations by Liberals we find the present Finance minister declaring in the budget speech that he is not only reducing the income tax 20 per cent but proposes to pursue a policy by which the income tax will be by degrees eliminated entirely. The hon. gentleman who now occupies the position of Speaker of this house supported the income tax in these words:
I warned my hon. friend a year and a half ago when he introduced his business profits tax that he would yet have to come to the income tax, which of all taxation measures is the most natural and fairest. According to the best authorities, such as Adam Smith and Thiers, the income tax is the least objectionable of all systems of taxation, because it makes no distinction as between the taxpayers.
Then further he says:
In spite of the hopes of my hon. friend, bright as he thinks they are, I really believe that the income tax has to-day entered into the politico-economic system of Canada, to stay there for many generations.
Those, Mr. Speaker, are the opinions, the policies, of those old-time Liberals, shall I say, who stuck to Liberal policies, Liberal principles and did not do as Goldsmith, I think, said:
Unskilful he to fawn, or seek for power,
By doctrines fashioned to the varying hour.
By those old Liberals, by those who stuck to Liberal principles and voted for them, the income tax was thought and said1 to be a sound economic Liberal principle, and it was expressly stated by them that reductions, if they
The Budget-Mr. Adshead

ever did take place, should take place not in the income tax but in the customs duties.
But I go still further. I notice that the Minister of Finance in addressing the interprovincial conference made some rather startling statements directly in connection with the question of the public debt and the income tax. On November 9, the Minister of Finance was discussing in the interprovincial conference the debt of Canada, and this is a precis of what he said:
The minister took the conference into his confidence with respect to the war debt which to-day amounts to $1,694,621,687 with an annual cost of carrying including fixed charges of $162,799,000. The special taxes imposed for the purposes of carrying this burden failed to meet it by the sum of over $6,000,000. The minister stated that out of the total cost of administering Canada, its railways, its canals, subsidies, etc., paid out since confederation, 36 per cent represented the cost of Canada in the War.
He went on further:
There had been nothing to do but to impose new taxes or to repudiate the debt.
Prior to the Minister of Finance suggesting or mentioning repudiation of debt at the interprovincial conference, the only mention I notice made of repudiation was in 1917. It must be borne in mind that the income tax was imposed for one purpose, namely, to pay the war debt, and it was to be left on until the war debt was paid. When the Minister of Finance states that he must seek for new taxes in order to meet those debts, I do not know wherein he is consistent when now he wants to abolish a tax which was inaugurated for the purpose of meeting the war debt. He goes on further and this statement of his is still more extraordinary:
The minister stated that Canada was faced with the following maturities:	1928,
$53,000,000; 1929, $60,000,000; 1930, $20,000,000; 1931, $77,000,000; and 1932, $73,000,000. He hoped that if revenues were maintained and the country continued to grow to materially reduce, if not retire all these obligations. The great difficulty came however in 1933 when the sum of $446,000,000 came due, and in 1934 when the sum of $535,000,000 came due. . . .
Coming to the much disputed question of the income tax, Mr. Robb dealt with the contention that it was opposed to the spirit of the British North America Act because it was an invasion of the direct field of taxation.
But this is tihe point. In face of all the statements made by those worthies of old who inaugurated the income tax for the express purpose of meeting the war debt and of the Minister of Finance himself acknowledging that the obligations which matured increased year by year and that in 1933 and 1934 the obligations which matured were so great that he hardly knew how to meet them,

except, as he stated, by imposing new taxes -in the face of all that, he deliberately, against the policy of the Liberal party, attempts not only to reduce the income tax by 20 per cent to-day but to continue reducing that very measure which was introduced into the house for the purpose of meeting war obligations.
How will these obligations be met if the income tax is wiped out by 1934? There is only one other way of meeting them and that is by means of customs duties, although the Liberal policy, as stated, proclaimed by the Liberal party, states that the income tax should be retained and that if any reductions are to take place they should take place not in the income tax but in the tariff. The minister made the further statement that we should not forget that in connection with the national debt the generation which spent the money should not shirk its responsibilities. In view of what I have stated; in view of what the policy of the Liberal party was when the income tax was inaugurated, and in view of the declarations of Liberal leaders that if there is any shirking of the payment of those obligations, I maintain the responsibility lies with those who have the most money with which to pay them, and that the burden should not be placed, as it is under the customs tariff, on the consumer who is the least, able to bear it.
Having put forward that argument, I make the plea that the income tax should not be reduced and that, if there is a way out without endangering the government or lowering its dignity, the 10 per cent which has been taken off should in some way be restored. It was with a heavy heart I heard the Minister of Finance declare that he was going to reduce the income tax by another 10 per cent, and that further reductions were going to be made, especially when I knew that this was contrary to true Liberal principles and to the ideals of those people who inaugurated the tax and supported it for the express purpose of meeting war debts and obligations. If the income tax had not been touched, speaking for nobody but myself, I should have seen my way to support the budget; but I feel, with the giving up of the absolute principles of Liberalism, I cannot support the budget and I must support the subamendment of the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Fansher).
Perhaps the Minister of Finance will consider the suggestion that in the committee he might add that 10 per cent on again, even if he distributes it to the provinces. The provinces claimed in the interprovincial conference that the income tax, being direct taxation,

The Budget-Mr. Adshead
belongs to them. The British North America Act however states that the federal government has a perfect right to enter any field of taxation it may desire. I believe there is a way out and moreover I feel convinced, if we really knew just the hearts and minds of my hon. friends opposite, there is a good deal of misgiving among those who may support the budget, that Liberal principles are being sacrificed, and the reduction in the income tax is not at all to their liking. They are perhaps in the unfortunate position of having to vote for something they do not like rather than embarrass the government, or would they rather embarrass the government and stand by their principles? I should not like to see the government turned out. It is unfortunate that sometimes we have to choose between one of two things, between violating our conscience and embarrassing the government, and sometimes as the lesser of the two evils we violate our conscience. In view of the fact that a 10 per cent reduction took place in the income tax last year, against which we protested strongly and moved an amendment which should have served as a warning to the government that such a practice would not be countenanced again so far as we were concerned, and knowing as I do the hearts and minds of the people of my constituency, the people of the Labour party, if you will, and all who are true Liberals, and who have expressed their opposition to any further reduction in the income tax, I feel that I should not be doing my duty to my conscience and towards my constituents if I did not oppose as strongly as I can this reduction.
I am sorry the Minister of Finance is not in his seat at the moment. The Minister of Railways was in the house a few minutes ago, but has gone out. I know that we back-benchers do not command very much attention, although we do get on Hansard. I am sorry the Minister of Finance is not here because I wish to refer to a statement that he made in Calgary last year. It was such an extraordinary statement that I took it up not only with my Labour friends but with my Liberal friends as well, and they were astonished because the minister's statement indicated to them, as it did to me, the attitude of the minister and his viewpoint on the income tax and incorporation tax. He made the statement that the reduction in the tax had saved to the corporations of this country $30,000,000, and went on to say that that $30,000,00 would no doubt gradually sift down right through to the man at the bottom. Unfortunately, that seems to be directly contrary both to Liberal principles
and the actual facts of the case. Mr. Bryan in that excellent book of his, The Crown of Thorns and Cross of Gold, made the statement that theTe were two methods of distributing wealth:	One was that it should
gradually sift down from the top to the person below, and the other was that it should go from the producers upwards until it reached those at the very top. It is evident that the latter way was the one the Liberals had in mind, whether or not that is their idea now, that the primary producers should first receive their share of the wealth they produce. But now we have the Minister of Finance say that the reduction, he had made in the tax had saved the corporations $30,000,000, which would no doubt sift down to the man below.
Dealing with the tariff for a few moments,
I was very glad to hear the excellent speech this afternoon of my hon. friend from South Huron (Mr. McMillan). He asked us why we did not go and sit over on that side of the house. We might equally well ask him why he does not sit over here. It does not matter where we sit; it is the principle we are supporting that matters. I assure him that if the gentlemen on his side will make a serious attempt to persuade the government of the necessity of putting Liberal policies into practice, he will receive all the support that it is possible for this section of the house to give, but he will not receive that support if the government simply go on year after year professing what we have heard to-day and for the last thirty years: Oh, these things cannot be done in a day; they must be done gradually 1 I heard that story, Mr. Speaker, thirty years ago in the province of Alberta, and we are still hearing it to-day. I say that action is necessary, that mere playing with the thing is not going to satisfy the members either of the Liberal party or those who sit over here. When I look over at that side of the house I see Liberals, Liberal-Progressives, Progressives, and in this section of the house Progressive and Labour. Why Progressives over there? Why do they not do as the hon. member for South Huron suggested, join up with the Liberal party? It was just because of the facts I have cited that the Progressives ceded from the Liberals because they felt in their hearts that the Liberal party was not carrying out their policies, and they wanted to see those policies carried out and brought to maturity. That is the reason why my friends over there called themselves Progressives, and that is why they do go so far even as not to attend the Liberal caucus.
The Budget-Mr. Adshead

Mr. Ewart, a gentleman well known in the city of Ottawa, made a very pertinent statement about the tariff, pertinent because true. He said that the Conservatives swore by the tariff, but were afraid to raise it, and the Liberals swore at the tariff, but were afraid to reduce it. I think that is a very true statement when we remember how few reductions have been made in the tariff since 1896, and since this government came into power the reductions have been almost infinitesimal.
I have not been able to examine all the new tariff schedules, but I have the opinion of the adviser of the Consumers' League, and he does not seem to be very favourably disposed towards the present tariff proposals of the government. He says that the general opinion is that there is a revision downward, but that that is a matter which can only be determined: by careful investigation. But this much is certain; there are changes upward, and there are changes downward. In some cases a higher rate of duty is changed on the higher priced product, the rate remaining unchanged on the medium priced article, and on the lower priced article the duty is lowered. The schedules in the intermediate tariff under which practically nothing enters the country are lowered materially, but the schedules under which importation takes place are only slightly reduced. This, Mr. Speaker, is not tariff adjustment; it is tariff legerdemain.
As regards the British' preference, although you have increased the British preference by 50 per cent, you have stipulated that at least 50 per cent of the product must represent empire labour and material. The cotton manufacturers of my native city of Manchester import nearly 30 per cent of the cotton products from the United States. Nearly all their cotton is imported from the United States and is manufactured in Manchester and the neighbouring towns. But if this 50 per cent provision as to empire labour and material is to be applied, their product will not be able to come in under the British preference, and will have to come in under the general tariff and pay a duty of 30 per cent. That would wipe out the British preference so far as cotton is concerned, and simply give added protection to the cotton manufacturers of Canada.
We have been told that this country is very prosperous. I agree that we are more prosperous than we were, but there has never been a time in the history of Canada when somebody was not prosperous. In our darkest hour in 1918, the Dominion Textile Company, which will benefit under these cotton schedules, earned 291 per cent while our boys were dying

in Flanders. They were prosperous. Sil Charles Ross was prosperous when afterwards, if I remember aright, he was voted' two million dollars in lieu of the profits that he might have made. Surely he was prosperous. I say there never has been a time, however dark nationally, when somebody in this country was not prosperous. But the idea of prosperity is not that it should be allotted to three or four or even twenty; true prosperity prevails only when it is spread among all classes so that even in the humblest shack of a settler in the far-away constituency of my friend from Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) its influence may be felt. And that, Mr. Speaker, is our idea of prosperity.
I do hope the government will see the folly of still reducing the income tax. I do hope they will realize that it is contrary-if I may recapitulate-to the declared principles of those great Liberal worthies whom hon. gentlemen opposite hold up as models of statesmanship-the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Mr. A. K. Maclean, the late Mr. Frank Carvell, and even Your Honour before you were called to the chair. All these influential leaders of the great Liberal party advocated the imposition of the income tax as a means to pay off the war debt. And yet the government have abandoned those principles and reduced the income tax. WTiat evil influence persuaded the Minister of Finance to take this course I know not, but I sincerely hope that some means will be found by which Liberal consciences, Liberal-Progressive consciences and our own may be satisfied, so that we can support the budget; in other words, I do hope that the government will maintain the income tax without change and thus put into practice Liberal policies and honour Liberal principles.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the member for East Calgary (Mr. Adshead), who has just taken his seat, will,
I am sure, excuse me if in my limited time I do not attempt to answer in detail the propositions which he has outlined in his interesting speech. But he asked one question which must have occurred to many other hon. members and to the people generally, and perhaps after he has been in this house longer he will become accustomed to the repudiations of policy, the violations of pledges and the inconsistencies he has pointed out in the record of the government. These departures from the often declared principles of the Liberal party can be explained only on the assumption that the conflicting views held by the members of the cabinet and by their supporters in this house cancelled one another, with the result that we do not get

The Budget-Mr. Stewart (.Leeds)
vigorous action on any line of policy; we do not get fulfilment of any of the pledges that have been given by the government in the past.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the budget is, of course, a review of the financial affairs of the Dominion for the past year. We take revenue and expenditure, assets and liabilities, and we analyze as far as we can the situation from that standpoint. In surveying our assets we must not overlook one of outstanding importance, our Canadian National railways, an organization that is extending its usefulness, improving its services and very materially bettering its financial condition as the years go by. That is a situation which must afford great satisfaction to the house and to the country at large. If we endeavour to analyze the causes of these results, I think we may fairly divide them in the proportion of about fifty-fifty between the able management that that organization has had under Sir Henry Thornton, and the loyal support and cooperation which he has secured from the large army of employees of that vast system. These two influences have resulted in increasing the revenue, decreasing the operating expenses, and leaving a very substantial surplus-a surplus that is continually growing larger and larger.
Some criticism has been directed against the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) for the way in which he has dealt with the financial obligations of the Canadian National Railways, or perhaps, more properly, I should say the financial obligations of Canada in relation to the Canadian National Railways; because, after all, Mr. Speaker, we own this great railway system, and its debts in the last analysis are therefore the debts of Canada. The member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) pointed out that if we took into consideration the financial obligations of the Canadian National Railways we would find that not only had we not decreased our national debt in the last few years, but that on the contrary it had been increased. In this connection it may be interesting to refer to the budget debate in the session of 1923, when the Right Hon. Mr. Fielding was finance minister. He had to deal with the indebtedness of the Canadian National Railways, and in Hansard for that year we find that in the course of his budget speech he said in relation to the Canadian National Railways:
We turn now to the year 1922-23, which closed not many days ago. We have not the complete accounts before us, but there is sufficient information to enable us practically to announce the result. Ordinary revenue amounted to $393,619,000. These are estimates, as the figures are not absolutely final.
Ordinary expenditure amounted to about $331,780,000. As between those two items, there was then a surplus of $61,839,000. Capital expenditure, however, represents $14,500,000; adjustment of war claims, $6,700,000; cost of loan flotations, $3,050,000; these representing in all $24,250,000. There was thus a surplus over ordinary, capital and special expenditures, of $37,589,000. But again the railways have to be taken into account. We had to advance during that year $92,190,000 for railways, and $6,060,720 for the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, making in all for that charge, $98,250,720. This, of course, takes up all the surplus I have mentioned and leaves a large balance on the other side of the account. If we take everything into consideration for the year, the net result was that we added to the public debt in the year just closed $49,293,086. The receipt of something over $8,000,000 from the British government on exchange account helped us to keep down what otherwise would have been a larger addition to the public debt.
The addition of nearly $50,000,000 to our public debt in the past year is not a situation that should cause very much satisfaction in any quarter.
That was the way Mr. Fielding reviewed the situation. In the following year we find the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) adopting an altogether different course. I quote from Hansard:
Turning now to the public debt. On March 31, 1923, our net public debt stood at $2,453,770,868.74. Our estimated ordinary revenue for the year just closed is $396,000,000. Our estimated ordinary expenditures of $328,250,000, and capital expenditures $12,170,000; special expenditures $8,390,000; railway loans $23,781,664; Canadian government merchant marine loans $1,500,000, and loans to Quebec Harbour Commission, which are treated as a non-active asset, $500,000, together with an amount of $621,987 carried on the books of the department for Victoria Shipowners, Limited, which it is proposed to treat as a non-active asset in the place of an active asset as heretofore, make the total charges $375,213,651. Our surplus of ordinary revenue over these expenditures will therefore be $20.7S6.349 to be applied towards the reduction of the national debt as it stood on March 31, 1923. To this must be added $1,317,000, being the amount of sundry outstanding indebtedness cancelled during the past year, and a further amount of $8,305,760.37 received in settlement of an adjustment of acknowledged book debts between the imperial and the dominion governments. These two amounts, totalling $9,622,760.37, together with the $20,786,349 surplus of revenue over total
. [DOT] .	1	1	_..1*1 1 n /I nL4" n o AT
These figures show that with a revenue of $393,000,000 odd, and taking into consideration the situation of the Canadian National Railways, the Right Hon. Mr. Fielding found that the debt of Canada was increased by $50,000,000, while his successor, the present Minister of Finance, with a revenue of $396,000,000, almost the same, finds that our pub-

The Budget-Mr. Stewart {Leeds)
lie debt is reduced by about $30,000,000. It is perfectly clear that these two gentlemen have adopted different methods of procedure in dealing with the revenues of Canada and the expenditures and obligations of the Canadian National Railways. The explanation is found in the fact that in the year 1923 an amendment to the Canadian National Railways Act was passed, permitting the government to guarantee securities issued on behalf of the system; and since that legislation was enacted the government have adopted the principle of guaranteeing the obligations of the national railways and then forgetting all about it when coming to deal with the liabilities of Canada at the end of the year. The Canadian National Railways sign on the face of the bond, the Minister of Finance signs on the back of the bond, and then, like our old friend Micawber, the government says, "Thank the Lord, that debt is paid." The indictment of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George in respect of this feature of our financial situation stands unanswered.
We hear a good deal about the prosperity of Canada, and in support of the contention that we are really prosperous we are supplied with (the statements of bank managers and of financial organizations. These statements are all very well in a way, but I have no doubt they are as optimistic as the circumstances will permit; they have the perfectly proper and legitimate purpose of stimulating and encouraging business. I think, however, it is well that the house should note one sentence in the speech of the mover (Mr. Ilsley) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne-a very able speech. He says:
In discussing the question of Canada's prosperity, Mr. Speaker, there is one unfavourable feature which should be mentioned, and that is the fact that this prosperity has not been as evenly distributed as might have been the ease, or as we would have liked to see it. 1 am not now referring particularly to the distribution as between classes in the community, although a good deal could be said as to that; I am referring to the territorial distribution of prosperity in which the people m the maritime provinces, unfortunately, have been slow to share.
Apparently, therefore, this prosperity, according to one of the supporters of the government, is not as general as we could hope it to be. We all rejoice in the prosperity of Canada; we are not going to disparage or minimize it. It is inevitable that, as we advance from our war difficulties, from the difficulties of deflation, our condition will improve. We have had good harvests and good prices. But, I submit, no gentleman in this 
house has in any direct or tangible way connected the prosperity of Canada with the policies of this government, and it is impossible to do so. The prosperity is positive, and it would be much greater if in this country of vast natural resources we had a government with the courage to evolve and put into force some policy that would conserve and develop these resources for the benefit of the Canadian people. After all, no country of the size of Canada, possessing the vast resources which we have, can be truly said to be prosperous when fifty or sixty thousand of its best people have annually to leave that country to seek their home in a foreign land.
We are of course reminded of the tax reductions, and the outstanding feature in the reduction of the sales tax is the fact that it is taken off little by little. The result is that the consumer does not profit by these trifling reductions. If the sales tax were removed at once and made effective within a few months, and there were no loss to the merchants, then there would be an immediate and practical benefit to the consumers of Canada. It must be recalled, of course, that the sales tax, if the reduction now proposed goes into effect, will then be only where it was when this government came into power in 1921. The stamp taxes, which have disappeared, were also put on to a large extent by this government, and we have the spectacle of an administration boasting of reducing taxes which it has itself imposed on the country.
I contend, Mr. Speaker, that so long as any government takes from practically the same number of people an amount of taxes increasing year :by year we cannot truthfully say there is any real reduction in taxation. In looking up the reports I find that in the fiscal year 1926 the revenue from taxation amounted to $327,575,000, in round figures. In 1927 the revenue from taxation amounted to about $346,650,000, while in 1928 it is estimated that the revenue from taxation will be about $357,000,000. The house will note an increase in the total revenue from taxation during these years, and when this amount is being taken from practically the same population there can be no real decrease in taxation. That contention is as hollow as a drum which may be gilded and beaten in order to provide music to which the supporters of the government may march. It may be sufficient for that purpose, but after all it does not provide very pleasant music for the people of Canada.
We have in this budget a revision of some items to a certain extent. I do not propose to go into those in detail, but after all it

The Budget-Mr. Stewart (Leeds)
is really interesting to review the record of this government in connection with the tariff, because it illustrates in a most striking manner that inconsistency to which the last speaker referred. I sat in the gallery of this house before 1921 and heard the present Prime Minister vigorously demand a general downward revision of the tariff all along the line, and I am sure he went through the country giving that as the policy of the Liberal party. The first budget presented after he came into power was in 1922, and if one only had time it would be interesting to read Hansard and quote some of the statements made in connection with that budget. It is true that there were some revisions, but it was a disappointment to those who expected the promise of the Prime Minister to be fulfilled. His supporters were pacified to a certain extent, however, by the hope that it was only a beginning, and that it was a step in the right direction. Then we had the budget of 1923, in which the then Minister of Finance said we must have tariff stability; that the business interests of Can-must not be disturbed from time to time by these reductions; that the tariff after all was a moderately low tariff, and that if business were to prosper there must be stability of tariff. There were no tariff reductions that year. In 1924 we find another step taken in the direction of reduction, and in 1925 we find the excuse advanced that the tariff board was appointed and therefore the government must wait for the decisions of that board. In 1926, on the eve of an election, we had some reductions in tariff without waiting for the decisions of the tariff board, because it was thought that these reductions would be helpful. In 1927 the government apparently took another backward step; there \yere no changes in the tariff. In 1928 we have some changes, the effect of which I am not prepared to state because I have not been able to analyze them sufficiently in detail.
There is one reduction in this tariff, Mr. Speaker, to which I wish to refer, however, and to which I most emphatically object. I refer to the reduction in the tariff on dairy products coming into this country, particularly the products of Australia and New Zealand which enter our market to compete with the product of our dairy farms. According to the Dairy News, a letter issued from the Department of Agriculture under date of February, 1928, we find that in the year 1927 there came into this country 11,208,819 pounds of butter, while in 1926 we imported 9,151,882 pounds. This is against a tariff wall of only one cent per pound, and of course
there has been a storm of protest from the dairying interests of this country. I have moved for a return showing these protests, and when they come down I am sure they will be very interesting indeed. These protests come from all parts of Canada, and before this debate is over I should like to hear from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) how he justifies a reduction which is working such injury to the interests that it is his duty to protect and care for.
In connection with the tariff one is interested in the pronouncements of the present Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler) before he assumed that office. We find that in the year 1924, speaking on the address, he said:
I do not know what there is to be gained at the present moment by the making of slight tariff changes. A policy of nibbling has never appealed to me.
He goes on to state that he approves of stability in the tariff, and continues:
Let me say to possible critics of my attitude on the tariff when considered in conjunction with the tariff platform of 1919. I did not support that platform; I never endorsed it and I have on two occasions repudiated it in this house. I do so again now.
Then he announces his intention of voting against the budget. I suggest that if he is to be consistent he will vote against this budget on the same ground. This is a nibble at the tariff, and a big nibble to the prejudice of the dairying interests of this country. I should like to hear from the Minister of National Revenue as well, before the debate is finished.
We have heard a great deal, Mr. Speaker, about wider markets. If we look at the trade returns of this country, as published by the Department of National Revenue, we find that our imports in 1927 were greater than in 1926. In 1926 our total imports amounted to $2,256,028,869, while in 1927 their value was $2,298,465,647, and when we look at our exports we find that in 1926 they amounted to $1,328,700,137, while in the year 1927 they were valued at $1,267,573,142. There are, of course, two markets for the Canadian people the foreign market and the home market. Those who have dealt with the treaties that have been adopted by this government have proved conclusively that we are not gaining very much in the foreign market, while the figures I have quoted establish beyond all doubt that we are narrowing and contracting the home market, which after all is the most reliable and the best. In foreign markets we have to meet the competition of the world. Changing policies and changing

The Budget-Mr. Stewart (.Leeds)
conditions make this market erratic and unreliable. In, no instance are the conditions satisfactory.
With regard to immigration, the volume of disinterested and intelligent criticism that has grown up in this country must convince us and the people at large that our policy in this respect is very largely a failure. We are spending many millions to bring people to this country, and we are losing from sixty to seventy thousand of our population annually to the United States. Some say they are coming back. Yes, Mr. Speaker, they come home for Christmas and they go back for the new year. After making every allowance, the figure that I have mentioned' is a fair representation of our total annual loss. We are opening the front door to those coming from other countries, and we are leaving the side door open for the escape of our own people, the best asset we have, in the numbers that I have mentioned to the adjoining country. The situation demands heroic treatment. Some solution must be found. In view of our peculiar conditions we may be driven to adopt export duties, embargos, bounties, and wherever necessary higher import duties, in order that we may conserve and develop our natural resources as far as possible in Canada and for the benefit of our own people.
There is one subject of absorbing interest, Mr. Speaker, with which I should like to deal if time permitted, and which I must discuss very briefly. That is the St. Lawrence development. No mention of it has been made in the speech from the throne, but it is of absorbing interest because of its extent and its direct relation to the prosperity of the country. We have had boards, we have had joint boards, we have had advisory committees and reports galore, but no action has been taken. Let me say that although vitally interested in this project I do not urge any hasty or ill considered action, but I am anxious that Canadian interests shall be fully protected. The development will involve a considerable period of time, and we may well be excused for urging that there should be no delay. The matter has been referred to the courts. If I have any criticism to offer in this connection it is that the reference seems rather involved, and when the proceedings are finished I am afraid it will be necessary for the conflicting interests to arrive at some agreement before anything can be done. If this work is undertaken and carried to a conclusion let me urge that it be done as soon as possible and the whole of it developed concurrently; not without completing one section in one province to the detriment of another section in another pro-

vinoe. When the project is carried out it will bring traffic to our railways, it will attract thousands of people to our country, it will give an impetus to agriculture, and it will make of the valley of the St. Lawrence the most extensive and intensive industrial area in the world; and while, as I have said, we do not urge haste we suggest that action should be taken at the earliest possible moment. Let me point out that when this development comes to the international section the opportunity may be afforded to correct the errors which appear to have been made in connection with the Chicago drainage matter. We trust the scheme will be carried out as far as possible in Canadian territory and by Canada; we are not in favour of joint development except where absolutely necessary.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I must conclude. There is an amendment before the house which reads:
This house regrets that the measures proposed by the government do not tend to provide increased employment in Canada, nor to induce the return of Canadians to their native land, nor to prevent the continued emigration of our people to the United States; and that they make no provisions for the preservation of our domestic markets for Canadian farm and dairy products, nor for the effective development of the natural resources of the country, nor for the abolition of the sales tax by the 1st of January, 1929.
I propose to vote against this budget and for this amendment, and I wish to consolidate my reasons for so doing. I have tried to show that on a proper consideration of all our obligations we have an increasing and not a decreasing debt. If all the obligations we have are taken into account we will find that in the last four or five years our debt has been increased by $40,000,000 instead of decreased as contended by the Finance minister. I have shown that during these few years we have been taking each year an increasing amount in taxation from the Canadian people, and my argument is that instead of there being a decrease in taxation there is an increase. I have shown by the figures from the Department of National Revenue that our export trade is decreasing, and that we are increasing the importation into this country of goods which should be made at home. I have shown that the home market, which is the most desirable and the best market for the Canadian people, is being invaded. Furthermore, instead of our markets abroad being widened, they are being contracted, and at the same time the home market is being opened to competitors who are coming in and taking possession of it to the detriment of our own people. The

The Budget-Mr. Edwards (Waterloo)
figures that the government have' produced show conclusively that we are losing population at the rate of sixty or seventy thousand a year. The government, I think, is gambling to a large extent with Canada's prosperity, and is neglecting to lay down any permanent policy which is calculated to lead to improvement. It is following a policy of nibbling at the tariff which is distressing to industry and to agriculture, and is gradually undermining the foundations upon which our material prosperity rests. For these reasons I shall vote for the amendment and against this budget.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to offer my contribution to the debate on the budget I fully realize that the ground has been pretty well covered by hon. members who have preceded me, but the viewpoints as expressed by hon. gentlemen are of course widely divergent in character, this, I presume, being caused by the varied interests that exist throughout this great country. Those who come from the prairie provinces naturally have the viewpoint of that section; those from the provinces down by the sea have their problems, namely, those of the steel and iron industry, the coal industry and other industries indigenous to that part of Canada, while we in the central provinces have problems dealing more particularly with industrial and agricultural matters.
Before proceeding further I should like to take advantage of this my first opportunity to compliment the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler) upon, his elevation to that high office. We in the county of Waterloo-and I have the honour jointly to represent the good county of Waterloo with the Minister of National Revenue-are very proud of the honour that has come to him, and we in the southern portion of the county desire to congratulate him and to wish him every success. I feel sure that he will fill the position with great credit to himself and also to the state. He is an able native son of our county. With the influence which I presume he has with this government it seems to me that he might have been a little more successful in protecting some of the industries which are established in the southern part of the county and which have been very badly hit by this budget. I refer more particularly to the textile industries, those of
woven cloths and worsteds. This question however I will take up at greater length later on.
AVith the reduction in the sales tax, as shown in this budget, I am in hearty accord As this tax is a burden upon the masses of the people, upon all consumers rich and poor alike, I hope the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) will take it into his serious consideration and endeavour to wipe out the sales tax by the end of the current year.
Much has been said about our national debt. To the best of my knowledge and ability to calculate the amount of this debt, we are $20,000,000 worse off to-day than we were when this government took office. Possibly I should not say worse off, because we have not yet been given an account of the tangible assets of the Canadian National Railways for which I presume the money was granted. There are, however, different viewpoints on the subject, but it seems to me a matter of book-keeping whether or not the loans made to the Canadian National railways should be included in the national debt of this country. They are obligations on the country just as much as any other obligation and they should be so recorded.
In the constituency of South AVaterloo which I have the honour to represent in this house we have the happy combination of a splendid agricultural section and a well organized and highly industrialized district with a varied line of manufactured products, including the iron and steel industry in its many different lines, furniture factories and their subsidiaries, large shoe factories, textile factories, including woollen and worsted cloth mills, knitted goods, silk yarn, and silk cloth manufactures. It will be readily seen that any variation in tariff schedules is more or less reflected in conditions in this constituency. We have employed in South Waterloo in the textile factories upwards of 3,500 hands. This is the number of the actual workers in this industry exclusive of their dependants, and therefore hon. members will realize that anything that injures this industry is of very serious moment to our part of t'he country.
With reference to the so-called review made of the textile industry by the tariff advisory board I wish to make a few remarks. All branches of this important industry placed their positions in facts and figures before this board and all that was expected was a square deal with reference to tariff adjustment based upon the facts and figures presented. If this course had been followed and the Minister of Finance had been guided by this in the formulation of his budget, no debate on the woollen goods industry would
732	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Edxoards (Waterloo)
have been required at this time. All that is asked by the textile trade or any other industry I know of is to be placed in a position where they can compete on even terms with outside competitors. They are not asking favours; they are not asking any special considerations; they are not asking any high tariff adjustments. What they are asking is that the workers in this country be privileged to compete with workers in outside countries on even terms and nothing more. When we have regard to living conditions brought about in certain other countries by low wages; when we consider such safeguards as the eight-hour day in many lines; the minimum wage law; the Workmen's Compensation Act; safety devices of various kinds which are designed for the protection of the workmen and which are compulsory, humane and necessary; child labour laws; the Old Age Pension law-which I hope will soon be enacted in Ontario-when we consider all these safeguards with which industry is surrounded in this country, it will, I am sure, be readily seen that some protection must be given to Canadian industry to enable it to meet conditions imposed, so that it will not be forced to face unrestricted competition from England, France, Belgium or elsewhere, where like conditions do not obtain.
Let me take the weekly wages of textile workers in Canada as averaged from figures supplied by Canadian mills and compare them by hours of labour and sex of worker with those of workers in the mills of Yorkshire, England. The figures are as follows:
