These figures were gathered at the end of 1924 a*d the comparison is made with wages in Canada in 1924. It is only fair to state that since that time wages in Canada have been reduced by ten per cent. These figures are not guess work; they were obtained by me from the books of the mills. I quote from the budget speech, as follows:
It is proposed to aid the Canadian weaving industry by granting free yarns for weaving purposes.
That particular branch of the industry that is engaged in the weaving of woollen cloths
[Mr. A. M. Edwards. [
and worsteds is the one to which I wish to draw the attention of hon. members, in order to show how it will be affected by this budget.
Previous to this budget, knitted yarn coming into this country, what is called forties and finer, used in the weaving of woollen and worsted cloths paid a duty of 12J per cent. Under the new tariff schedule these yarns come in free, and I wish to show how that change is going to affect the industry in South Waterloo. In the first place there is, I understand, only one mill in Canada making cloth that does not spin its own yarn. This one mill, situated in Toronto, will be in the position of being able to purchase its yam from England at a low price. But what of the other mills? I am thinking now more particularly of two of the larger mills in my constituency, one located in the town of Hespeler and the other in the town of Preston; and these are typical examples showing how this particular industry will be affected not only in the constituency of South Waterloo but elsewhere in Canada. One of these mills employs between 1.000 and 1,100 hands, and the other is actually employing at the present time 228 hands. Both these mills begin with the raw product-the wool-and work it through the different processes up to the finished cloth. I would like hon. members to observe how this help is divided between male and female. In the case of the mill employing the 228 people there are 68 men employed in carding, spinning and preparatory operations, and 22 women; in the warping, weaving and finishing departments, there are 35 men, and 103 women. These figures cover the actual workers in these departments at the present time and do not include workers classed as "overhead"; in other words, the wool is taken in at one end of the mill, and it is washed and combed and carded and spun into yarn. In that process a lot of men helpers are required, but after it passes that stage the material goes into the loom and is woven into cloth, and these looms are largely tended by female workers, so that anything you do that injures the original part of this business, the converting of the raw wool into the yarn, affects the heads of families more than would a change that was applicable to the later processes.
The amount paid for carding, spinning and preparatory operations, including overhead, is 40^ per cent of the total wages paid. I would like hon. members to take note of that fact, that when these new schedules come into operation, out of every $100 that these mills are to-day paying in wages approximately $60 will be paid in the mills, and $40 will be sent

The Budget*-Mr. Edwards (Waterloo)
to other lands. That gives you some idea of the injury that will be done to this business.
The value of the machinery and housing for this particular mill of 228 people which I have mentioned, if it is to be scrapped, will be between $400,000 and $500,000.
I now come to the larger mill employing between 1,000 and 1,100 hands, and in this connection I propose to read a letter I received from the general manager of this company.
I had written and asked him to let me know just how his mill would be affected. Let me say first that this mill is located in a town of 3,500 people, and when a mill employing between 1,000 and 1,1000 hands in a municipality of that size is injured you can see how seriously it is going to affect that community.
This is the reply I received from the general manager of this mill:
We have been going over our records here very carefully, and last year (1927) exactly one-third of our spinning department was employed in making yarns for weaving purposes, and as nearly as we can estimate it not 5 per cent of this plant is likely to be operated for weaving yarns under the new regulations of free yarns for weaving purposes allowed into Canada from (treat Britain, and there is positively no prospect of employing this part of our plant on other kinds of yarn, for the reason that there are other spinning plants in Canada who will be cut out of a certain amount of their yarn business by the new regulation and they will be forced to go after the knitting yarn business to a greater extent than before in order to keep operating, and we cannot hope to get knitting yarn business to take up the slack in our weaving yarn department. It is not only our plant in Hespeler that we are concerned about, but also our spinning mill in Orillia.
We are not denying that the weaving trade in Canada may possibly get some advantage by the change in the tariff on weaving yarns . from 12J per cent to the free list, but the advantage will be entirely at the expense of the spinning industry and those employed in the preparation of the wool through all the processes up to spinning, including sorters, scouring hands, card room hands, gill minders, combers, drawing room employees, spinners and twisters, and not only the above but labour employed in the dyeing department will also be affected because of the fact that much of the yarn required in weaving is in mixture effects, greys and coloured twists, etc., and the stock for these will have to be dyed in England before the material is manufactured or spun, so that the people employed in the dyeing _ in Canada will be hard hit also. We are going to be in the position of having all of these departments working at a discount, or in other words only partially employed, increasing the overhead charges in every one of these departments on the material which we will be able to continue to make. And as I explained to you when we were talking over the situation, the difference in wages which will be paid in our mills in the production of our cloth by manufacturing from imported yarns instead of
manufacturing the raw wool through all the processes into finished cloth will be m the proportion of 59 to 100; that is, where we would be paying $100 to our employees for manufacturing the goods from raw wool Canadian labour under the new arrangement will receive only $59, and the rest of the labour involved will be paid for in England.
If this is a good stroke of business tor Canada, we confess we are quiet incompetent to see it.
What we asked of the tariff board was a reasonable increase in the duty against finished cloth to enable us to carry on all the operations in Canada and employ people in this country. What we are getting from them apparently is nothing of the kind, but is a cutting away of the foundations of the Canadian weaving business and placing a large percentage of our operations on a free trade basis, the principle of which, if correct in connection with the spinning trade, should be equally correct in connection with the weaving trade.
The sacrificing of the spinning branch of the cloth trade in Canada we consider is utterly unwarranted from any practical standpoint, and particularly from the standpoint of the position which the country would find itself in in case of another war such as we have passed through, or which would cut off from Canada a supply of weaving yarns for any extended period of time. A strike in England in the spinning trade would be equally effective in closing up our weaving industry in Canada when our own spinning is in the discard, as it undoubtedly will be as a result of this type of tariff policy.
While we have stated that one-third of our plant is affected, the reason that the entire plant is not affected in the same way is that we are manufacturers of knitted goods as well as woven goods, and a mill which is exclusively in the weaving trade would be affected to at least 50 per cent of its equipment while we are affected to the extent of only about 33J per cent.
I might explain that there is no change in the tariff on spun yam that goes in to the ordinary textiles, such as knitted goods, and that has reference to coarser than 40's.
The two mills which I have taken are fair illustrations of this type of mill, namely, those that make cloth throughout Canada. It will therefore be seen what a serious matter it will be if these mills have to go out of the spinning of yarn for doth. It will be noted that the larger percentage of men workers is in the departments that are affected by the budget, that is, the carding and spinning departments, the operations from there on being mostly done 'by female workers, as the figures show. We are therefore taking the work from the heads of families-a most serious condition indeed. Let us suppose, for instance, that finding themselves unable to spin yam profitably for the weaving trade, these mills turn to the spinning of yam for the knit goods trade. The ultimate will be a large surplus of machinery to take care of existing consumption, and we have the ridiculous clause in the proposed tariff

The Budget-Mr. Edwards (Waterloo)
schedule allowing us to bring in textile machinery free of duty. Who under heaven wants textile machinery when there will be thousands of machines in this country lying idle?
Now let me deal with diy spun yarns to show how inconsistent this tariff schedule really is. This type of yarn has -been imported on a duty basis, subject to a drawback when converted into stockinette hosiery, and so forth. This drawback has been cancelled, to become effective in October next. In other words, dry spinning plants from October on will have the benefit of a duty of ten per cent where previously those yams came in free on the drawback plan. This policy is directly opposite to that pursued allowing yarns into Canada free of weaving. There are but two plants in Canada making this yarn, one in Hamilton, and the other in Toronto. The government apparently is desirous of building up a dry-spun yarn business for two manufacturers, but is not in favour of the same policy for yarn spinners using their own production for weaving.
With regard to cotton yams, fine cotton yarns 40's count and finer-made by only one mill in Canada, that is at Three Rivers- are now subject to duty, whereas up till now they have been free. This also is directly opposite to the action applied to yarns entering Canada for the weaving trade.
I have endeavoured, Mr. Speaker, to place before the house as best I can the effect which the proposed changes in the tariff will have upon the woven goods branch of the textile industry of Canada. Let us now see how far-reaching the results will foe by consulting the Preliminary Report on the Woollen Textile Industry in Canada, as issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce. Referring only to woollen cloth mills, there are fifty-seven mills in Canada making woollen cloth and, with one exception, all spinning their own yarn. These mills are situated: In Nova Scotia, 3; in New Brunswick, 2; in Quebec, 10; in Ontario, 42. The amount of capital invested in the manufacture of woollen cloth alone is $21,342,909, with 4,026 employees. These figures do not by any means indicate the amount invested or the number of people employed in all the textile factories-that is, the figures I have given the house are only for the woven trade. For the textile factories engaged on knitted goods, and so on, the figures are: Capital invested, $42,215,208; employees, 11,017. The value of the products produced, by provinces, was as follows in 1925:
Canada total	 $15,499,326
Ontario	 12,982,583
Quebec	 2,058,704
Nova Scotia and New Brunswick	458,039
[Mr. A. M. Edwards. [
The cost of the raw material entering into these finished goods was $9,415,211, and the value added by the process of manufacture was $6,084,115. Surely this is an industry that should merit careful consideration by those who have to do with the tariff.
I wish now to refer to one other branch of the textile trade, namely, that in connection with the manufacture of tapes, woven labels, and so on. These woven labels with the firm's name are attached to articles of clothing, and so forth. In the city of Galt there is an industry manufacturing this line of goods, established fourteen years ago. Under the existing tariff it has gradually expanded and worked up a fair business, and to-day it is employing seventy hands. It has not yet paid a dividend, profits being used for necessary expansion, the management realizing that in order to make money on a small business of this type it is necessary to put it on a first-class production basis, and in order to do this they have purchased additional equipment from time to time until now they are in a good position to carry on. When I tell the house that last year they made a little over nine thousand dollars profit it will be seen that they are not exploiting their tariff protection. Under the new schedule not only is the duty lowered on the finished product, but a duty is actually added to the raw material, which is cotton yarn. So you see they get it going and coming. On the basis of the 1927 business the increase in the cost of yarn to this institution will amount to $2,943, and the loss on sales through their being compelled to reduce prices to meet British and foreign goods will be $6,440-or a total loss, presuming business to be the same this year as in 1927, of $9,383. This will more than wipe out the entire profits of that institution for last year. If the proposed changes come into force this firm will have to discontinue business in the manufacture of tapes, causing a great financial loss and throwing many employees out of work.
To show who benefits by this cut in the tariff on tape, there is a small concern in the town of St. Mary's in the constituency of my hon. friend from South Perth (Mr. Sanderson), who spoke yesterday and was quite critical in his treatment of the speech made by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion). The concern to which I refer is a branch of an American mill. Their raw material is tape. Under the provisions of the tariff before this proposed change, they had to pay a slight duty on tape, which is their raw material. They put fasteners on the tapes and with a very slight operation they become their finished product, covered

The Budget-Mr. Edwards (Waterloo)
by patents. Now, under this arrangement they are able to bring their tapes in direct from the parent mill across the line. I ask hon. gentlemen opposite if this is the way to foster Canadian industry? Is this the way to take care of our working people?
To give the house some idea of how this budget is considered by the executives of these concerns, let me quote, from the Guelph Mercury of February IS, 1928, certain interviews given to that paper by the heads of several large concerns:
The spinning business of this city has been badly hurt by the Robb budget, according to Mr. Harry Quarmby, president and general manager of tlie Guelph Carpet Mills and the Guelph Worsted Spinning Mill.
"We have an expensive spinning plant here, with the latest equipment for the spinning of yarns, and all this could be scrapped and the hundreds of people turned out of employment because of the admission into Canada of yarn at the reduced rate provided for in the budget.
"It would seem that the government of Canada is more interested in keeping the wheels of industry in England turning than in Canada, so far as the yarn spinning industry is concerned, but that is of no benefit to Canadian work people.
"The new rates will mean that the orders now on hand for weaving yarn may be cancelled and no more orders received. What that means can be easily imagined by the citizens of this city and by the two hundred employees of the spinning department. The government of Canada has shown absolutely no sympathy for this business.
"Labor in England is poorly paid in comparison with that of like occupations in Canada. The result of this is that yarn can be spun in England, shipped to Canada and laid down in Guelph cheaper than it can be spun here. That requires no wizard to understand the logical result of the government's policy. It means ruin to the spinning industry. I cannot condemn the budget sufficiently so far as the Guelph yarn spinning business is concerned, and what applies to Guelph applies to all the yarn spinning plants in Canada," said Mr. Quarmby.
Hespeler Plant Will Feel It.
Mr. D. N. Panabaker, director of the Forbes Mill at Hespeler, called on by The Mercury, states that there are three hundred people employed in the yarn departments of the big mill.
"The budget is a very serious thing for Hespeler. Just what plan of action will be decided upon cannot be said at the moment. It will make a difference in the cost of cloth, but it is destructive to the spinning end of the big textile industries.
"There are no compensation clauses in the budget," said Mr. Panabaker. In England, according to a report published in February, the wages of spinners while 160 per cent higher than before the war. are still less than 60 per cent of the wages paid to the spinners and carders in Hespeler, and there is no possibility of competing with that handicap.
"Our plants are fully equipped with expensive machinery, and while the new budget permits machinery to come into Canada free, it is of no benefit to us, because already equipped. The tariff advisory board is fully acquainted with
the position of the spinning industry, but is powerless to make any redress. Hespeler will be hard hit, but we cannot tell yet just what procedure is to be followed," said Mr. Panabaker.
General Conditions.
Textile trades are badly worried because of the changes made in tariff. There has been a reclassification under cottons, woollens, silk, linen and hemp. There has been a reduction from 374 per cent to 30 per cent on some cotton duties, but on cotton yarn of 40 counts or finer, there has been imposed a duty under the general tariff where formerly it was free. The general effect of the cotton revision will be to increase the cost of cotton yarns to Ontario manufacturers.
Woollen Mills in Bad Way.
David C. Dick, president of the Canadian Woollen Manufacturers' Association, expressed regret that there was nothing in the latest Robb budget which would seem to be likely to help the old-fashioned woollen mills of Ontario. He said these -were in bad shape.
Mr. Dick said that free machinery from England would not help these mills very much, and as for free yarn, he did not believe that, from the very nature of their business, the old-fashioned woollen mills could buy yarn. Mr. Dick doubted very much whether the weaving mills would benefit one half of one per cent under the Robb proposals.
So far as the old-fashioned small mills, scattered all over the Dominion, where they weave woollen cloth, there are at the present time 20 of them, with 350 looms closed down, in the other 34 mills, with 1,015 looms, over half of the looms are standing idle. In Ontario the situation is extremely bad.
Means Unemployment.
Every weaver of worsted cloths in Canada, with one exception, has its own spinning plant to produce the yarns. If they take advantage of the free yarns, then, according to one of the best authorities in the business, it will mean the scrapping of hundreds of thousands of dollars' worth of machinery, and the throwing out of work of hundreds of employees.
The Robb budget will adversely affect the spinning plants of Canada, which produce worsted yarns to the extent of $500,000, in the opinion of one closely in touch with the situation.
Good-Bye To Lamb Chops.
Another result of the Robb Budget, according to one who has studied the matter, will be that the sheep industry will suffer tremendously.
"If free yarns are admitted, then the Ontario farmer will not find any market for his wool," said this authority. "It will mean that the farmer will not be able to afford to raise sheep. The result will be that you won't be able to buy a Canadian lamb chop on the market. The people of Canada will have to content themselves with eating frozen chops and Australian rabbits."
There are several others but I will not quote further; what I have read will give the house an idea as to just how these proposed changes in the tariff will affect these industries. In the large mill at Hespeler, which I know quite well, I saw huge bins of wool, one filled
736	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Edwards (Waterloo)
with an Australian product, another with New Zealand wool, and a third with Canadian. Not being sufficiently familiar with the business, I was anxious to know the proportion of Canadian wool that entered into their product, and how far the proposed tariff would affect the raising of sheep in this country. Accordingly I wrote to the general manager of the concern and to-day I have his wire in reply:
From careful investigation I can assure you that many carloads of Canadian wool have been consumed annually in cloth mills in your constituency. The effect of budget proposals will positively divert this wool from consumption in Canada. Industrial workers overseas and wool from foreign countries will undoubtedly be employed to the detriment of Canadian workers and displacing Canadian raw wool.
This will indicate what is likely to happen to the sheep trade in this country if the proposed policy is persisted in.
My time has about expired, but I hope I have placed fairly before the house the case of the spinning business, especially in relation to woollen and worsted cloth. I sincerely trust that the Minister of Finance will reconsider his decision to inflict upon this industry, involving hundreds of employees engaged in this class of work, a hardship such as I have pointed out. Not only is this continual tinkering with the tariff affecting the woollen and worsted cloth industry of Canada; it is actually frightening capital away from the country, because investors do not know which branch of industry will be attacked next. The result is that we have unstable and unsettled conditions all round.
I must conclude now, and in doing so I wish to thank the members of the house for the courteous hearing they have given me.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We had a promise from the government last year that when the tariff advisory board got under way the tariff would be revised, though cautiously, in a downward direction, so as to lower the cost of living. If the changes outlined in the budget now before us represent the work of the board, then I think the people throughout the country will be asking just what the board is doing . In my opinion the reconstruction of the tariff as outlined in the budget is not at all in accordance with the findings of the tariff advisory board. The country expected, as it had a right to expect, that now, ten years after the close of the war, which upset economic conditions for a period, something would be done to enable us to return to normal so far as the cost of living is concerned.
The hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Fansher) in his speech yesterday discussed
[Mr. A. M. Edwards. [
the way in which the Liberal party, the free trade party, has dealt with this great question, and I propose to adduce some facts to show why that party is pursuing its present course. Raw material under the budget is for the most part free again, but the consumer will have to pay a heavy penalty if he imports anything in the nature of a finished article. In some cases, I find, the intermediate and general tariffs are lowered, but the British preference remains as formerly. I find that item 537b, linen thread, is reduced, when imported from Great Britain, only 2 per cent. This is of value only to the importer; the consumer will reap no benefit. In items 569 a, b, c and d, which cover material for hats, the British preference remains the same but this material coming from other countries is taken off the free list and placed under a duty of 5 per cent and 7\ per cent under the general and intermediate tariffs respectively. The duty on the finished article in this case remains the same, at the prohibitive rates of 22J per cent, 27J per cent and 30 per cent. On inquiry I find that 90 per cent of this hat material comes from countries other than Great Britain, so the enmity to the British preference did not need to be emphasized here. It is evident also that those using this material are seemingly rather lacking in influence. It will be seen when we come to consider this budget item by item that in the importation of many articles in which the British manufacturer specializes the preferences hitherto enjoyed will not from now on apply, certain conditions making it impossible. This will have the effect of shutting out to some extent the British market for the agricultural products of the farmers of Canada.
Again, under item 267b I find a most amazing thing, the full import of which is not readily discerned. As far as I can see, the government has given notice to all small oil refining companies, and to those contemplating entering the business, to get out and stay out. In this connection I cannot help but think of the language used by Sir Richard Cartwright at the famous Liberal convention held in this city in 1893, when he said:
It must be obvious to everyone who will give the slightest attentive consideration to the working of the protective system in this country or elsewhere, that the moment you introduce that system you make legal provision for corruption on a most extensive scale.
I wonder what he would have said of these manipulations in favour of the Imperial Oil Company, let us say, or some of the other large concerns. However, it certainly presages more expensive gasoline for the general public.

The Budget-Mr. Evans
Taking it altogether, this budget is a rich man's feast. The money cost to the public through trade penalties has not been at all lessened, and the moral hazard has not been abated in any way. The income tax has been again lowered, but for the man who has no taxable income the burden has been increased, so far as I can find out. The parliament of Canada is the highest court in the land, the place from which one would suppose justice would emanate for all alike, but the present government, after having taken every possible means to inform themselves on the evil system of trade penalties, now come forth with a budget in defiance of that knowledge. This has given a direct challenge to the primary producers and workers of this nation; it has challenged the farmers to organize for political action, and it is even an invitation to the workers to strike for justice.
I have in my hand a pamphlet which has been presented to the government setting forth the demand of the farmers for free tools and implements, but the entire matter has been simply ignored. The farmers are the men who bear most of the burdens of this kind of state felony, but I am glad that there is at least one class remaining who have no desire to live on the sweated labour of any other class in Canada. The farmers of Saskatchewan have also asked for a freer method of distribution by the abolition of arbitrary valuations for customs purposes, which were designed to protect the large dealers, importers andi jobbers against cooperative companies.
I saw a resolution which was placed on the order paper by the hon. member for Wey-burn (Mr. Young), but since it has already been passed over twice it seems that he is not going to proceed with it, and the reason is obvious. Through party managers and manipulating politicians the government have become linked up with every concern in this Dominion with which they could make a bargain. That may be a rather harsh expression, but that is the way I look at it. Party funds have been subscribed by bootleggers, rum runners, distillers and others who want to defy the laws of this nation and of the United States. In this way these people purchase the legislation they desire, in order to evade the laws of this country. I make this statement on the authority of the report of the commission which has been lately printed, and if anyone wants a specific case he can turn to page 110 and read for himself. Again, the farming class of Canada has been farmed by the capitalistic class of this Dominion for the last forty years, and all governments of Canada for the last forty years, 56103-47
irrespective of party, have done the same thing. In this respect the present budget is no different from the budgets which have been presented in former years, but it does stamp this government as being composed of men who are willing to continue the sweated labour on the farms of Canada of our women and children, to say nothing of our men, to swell the profits of those who, through their henchmen in this house, proclaim their indolence, incompetency and callous indifference to the adverse economic conditions of all those other classes of the people who are practically reduced to the standard of slavery to satisfy their greed. The cotton manufacturers, the steel manufacturers and others come before the tariff board pleading for greater facilities with which to rob the public.
Here is one statement I do not like to make, but the Liberal and Conservative parties in this house to-day hold their offices as members of parliament and cabinet ministers by selling their power and influence. The report of the parliamentary committee appointed in 1926 to inquire into the customs irregularities, reveals the most astounding facts and it is for every patriot and honest man to take these facts into consideration here and now. The Western Producer, a Saskatchewan paper which was started some years ago to reflect the Progressive and economic thought of this Dominion, in its leading editorial of January 20, 1927, has this to say:
The Western Producer demands to know what individuals in the Canadian House of Commons owe their responsible office to money secretly contributed to a fund mysteriously spent.
At the sitting of the committee referred to, on June 11, 1926, after insistent questioning by the member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy), it came out that $274,000 had been subscribed to party funds and divided between both parties. In a clipping I have here from the Grain Growers Guide, the editor, who I think is very well known from one end of the Dominion to the other, has this to say:
The cases in question, where the evidence is indisputable, show contributions of approximately half a million of dollars from two concerns. It may be reasonably assumed that the campaign fund managers were equally busy taking contributions from all the other liquor interests, and that they must have gathered in at least $2,000,000.
Two millions of dollars! I ask, sir, what hope is there for Canada under these conditions? This money was to purchase the legislation desired. I say that this budget of to-day is a product of purchased power and influence. I wish to remind hon. members of a fact well within the memory of every

The Budget

Mr. Evans

man in this house, that not so long ago Sir Robert Borden read two men out of his party because of some irregularities in the sale of horses. The sale of the rights of men and women throughout Canada to-day goes merrily on, and not one in either of those two parties raises a voice on their behalf. Horse flesh, when considered from the political standpoint, is seemingly much more valuable than the lives of men and women.

speechtext:
Who is not a party to this
iniquitous system? I say it is time that hon. members declared themselves on this subject. This money has been divided between both parties. Whom do they represent in this house to-night? What have the heads of both parties to say to this, and will they take the means that Sir Robert Borden once took to purge their parties of these methods? It hurts me to make this statement, and it hurts worse from the fact that certain hon. members opposite have allied themselves with those who tolerate this system and benefit by it, members who once sat with us in this corner of the house.
I have another clipping in my hand from the Montreal Witness, that old journal which has for eighty years worked for righteousness in this country. In it there is given a list of firms which have evaded the payment of income tax to the extent of many millions of dollars; they were not even asked to make an income tax return. One of my neighbours when I lived on the farm, a poor devil who never had an income, who never had anything to pay income tax on, was sentenced to jail for thirty days at Prince Albert because he refused to make a return. He had to get somebody to do it for him, he did not even understand the English language. Yet the firms in question have not even been asked to make a return. Is this the Canadian parliament?
From the Saskatoon Daily Star, under date of June 14, 1927, I read the following:
fMr. Evans.]
It is estimated that as a result of the customs inquiry and the auditor's disclosures, three hundred millions will come into the treasury.
The farmers in this house have been accused of evading the payment of income tax. They never had any income to pay taxes on. In this budget the class which reduces the agriculturists of the Dominion to a state of dependence through budgets such as this is the one which is again relieved by law of the payment of a large portion of that tax, and the government is dependent on the tariff for revenue-a method which places at least $2 in the pockets of the protected manufacturer for every one that goes into the Dominion treasury. I need not go any further for authority on that point than to the Right Hon. W. S. Fielding, who was Minister of Finance in this government until a few years ago. Let me read his words:
It can be established positively, I believe, that if you take into account simply the difference between the duties that were paid during the period of the Liberal administration and the duties that would have been paid had the Conservative tariff remained in force, the money that went directly into the pockets of the Canadian people on that account alone was from $85,000,000 to $100,000,000. But it must be remembered-and economists, I think, will agree-that the saving you make in a case like that is not to be measured only by the amount that you did not pay into the customs; you have to take into account also the check that was put upon the rise of prices at home, and that for every dollar saved to the people in that direct way probably two dollars -were saved in the difference between the prices prevailing and those which would otherwise have been charged by the home manufacturer.

May 10, 1921. Now the
duties paid in 1921 amounted to 1794- millions. Twice that amount is over $359,000,000, and this is the amount that Mr. Fielding says the manufacturers added to the price to the Canadian consumer in disposing of goods sold in that year. The previous speaker, the hon. member for South Waterloo (Mr. Edwards), wants the whole of the difference between wages paid in Britain or other European countries and wages paid in Canada to be made up by the tariff. I ask: By what rule or reason can we shoulder the burden on to any other industry in this Dominion? The farmers, as I have already said, are the ones that carry the greatest part of this load. They sell their produce in the markets of the world, competing with Russia, China, India, Argentina, Australia, and in some of those countries they do not pay over one-sixth of the amount of wages which the Canadian farmer has to

The Budget-Mr. Evans
pay on his farm to get his wheat harvested. By what rule or reason can the hon. member shoulder that on to the agricultural class of this Dominion? Let me ask: By what rule or reason did the government decide to put a heavier burden this year on the agricultural class that is still labouring to make ends meet and failing as the days go by?
The Minister of Finance says: "Work and thrive." Our people are working on the farms of Canada to-day double the hours that are worked in the civil service and four hours longer than are worked by those in the cities who have the eight-hour day. Our women are on their feet at five o'clock in the morning and if they get their work done by nine o'clock at night they feel lucky. I ask again, and perhaps the Minister of Finance will answer me when he speaks: By what rule or reason does he maintain this trade penalty on the commodities which the farmer has to purchase? I find from this pamphlet presented to him and his colleagues this year that there is a duty on some of our articles amounting to 35 per cent. Is this reasonable? Show me that the agricultural class is to-day so prosperous that it can bear . the burden of all other industries. I challenge any member of the government side to-day to do that, and if I have time before I sit down I want to labour that point a little further.
A good deal has been made by the government this year regarding the reduction in the national debt. Debt is a relative matter and it must always be considered in relation to assets. The newspapers even have taken the matter up and much has been made of the fact that we have been able to meet maturing loans from current revenue. There are two ways of looking at this question. The minister gave us the impression, and the country has received it, that as a nation we are further away from a state of insolvency than we were last year. Is this so? I am more concerned to-day about our assets than our liabilities, and for this reason. In 1926 we sold 97,000 fewer finished cattle in the markets of Canada than we did in 1925, and in 1927 we marketed 21,282 fewer cattle than we did in 1926. But there is still another feature regarding agriculture that is worse even than the loss on finished cattle. 'In 1926 the farmers marketed 27,000 more calves than they did in 1925, and in 1927 they marketed 24,915 more than in 1926. Add to this the fact that matured cattle during this last year averaged twenty-five pounds each less in weight than the year before. The tremendous increase in the number of calves being marketed indicates that it will now be 56103-471
five or six years before the live stock industry regains its former status. Taken altogether, the diminishing live stock industry is a situation that should cause alarm to all who care for the development of this country, and not only its economic seriousness but its moral standard as well by the concentration of our workers in the centres of industry or the cities. The figures which I have given for 1927 in regard to the live stock industry I lately secured from the deputy minister of the department, Doctor Grisdale.
Between the years 1921 and 1926, two census years in Saskatchewan, despite all our immigration and despite the natural increase, we find that we had 2,000 fewer farmers in 1926 than in 1921 in that new province where the development in agriculture is chiefly taking place.

Two thousand fewer farm
holders. This fact regarding the number of farmers in Saskatchewan diminishing during that period by nearly 2,000 is surely conclusive evidence of the result of the traffic of the politicians in the lives of the workers. Our industrial lords and politicians may point to the building of great cities and their growth, but the foundations of cities lies in a contented, prosperous and virile population on the land. Destroy that foundation and the superstructure will tumble down on your own heads. Evil in every form by its very nature is its own avenger. The fact is that the government of Canada is had in tow by business interests, and this condition is of such long standing that even business is a secondary consideration to-day in the amassing of wealth.
The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) asks what this government has done for the mine owner, the manufacturer, and others, mentioning every activity in the Dominion-all going to show that business ability and courage are not the essentials in business to-day. The one essential, according to the hon. member for Fort William and some of his colleagues, is a successful linking up with the politician. Why?
The hon. member for Fort William also asks, what has the government done for the wage earner? Why does this government let our men go to the United States to seek work, he asks? The workingman has always been the concern of the patriotic protectionist, if you will let him tell the tale. Years ago I thought it was a patriotic thing to purchase my farm equipment from the factories
The Budget-Mr. Evans

of Canada. I have during my thirty-seven years of farming purchased three Chatham fanning mills. I had always thought that these fanning mills were made in Chatham, Ontario; but only lately I found out that the Chatham fanning mill is as often made in the United States or anywhere it can be made the cheapest. One of my friends who can vouch for this fact only lately came across from Windsor with four drayloads of Chatham fanning mills smuggled into Canada.

Was he a friend of

I would ask, where is the

The Chatham fanning mills are made in the city of Detroit, and I hope hon. gentlemen will get that right. These mills have always been protected by a high duty, for the sake of the workingman, I presume, but they can be smuggled into Canada under the pretence of their being unfinished articles.
The farmer was also a concern of the hon. member for Fort William, but I hope that our agriculturist population will never lose its self-respect to the extent of joining in the plea for political pilfer such as we hear in this house from members who declare their own inability to make their living.
Partyism-let me say a word regarding partyism. Party politics as it is carried on in this country is destructive to every good quality which we as a people should develop. The idea of the politician is to keep in power, but that politics should be dependent on business and business on politics to the extent it is, is evidence of a depravity that should at once be checked. The evil of this party system is seen only in its entirety when the government of a province is of the same political stripe as the one occupying the seats of power at Ottawa, and because of this-I wish the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) were in his seat-the people of Saskatchewan last year were humiliated and their sense of justice and freedom was ravished by the fact that the provincial police were used as stool pigeons to secure evidence to convict because a federal politician was concerned, an honest man who was not guilty.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I say that I listened carefully to the hon. member for Rosetown, and his charges were not directed against anyone in particular. It was just an insinuation that every member of this house was implicated except himself.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
All I have to say about this question of party funds is this: I am willing to join with the hon.

The Budqet-Mr. MacDonald (Cape Breton)
member for Rosetown in asking for a full investigation, because if there has been anything like that done, somebody on our side has been holding out. Many of us did not get our share, and I have no doubt that we had to contribute quite as liberally to our election expenses as did the hon. member for Rose-town.
Having listened to the last * two speakers, I rather sympathize with the Minister of Finance. They attacked him from entirely different angles, but I do not think he should have very much trouble in deciding which of the two criticisms is deserving of consideration. The hon. member for South Waterloo ('Mr. Edwards) presented facts and figures as to the exact effect that the proposed modifications in the tariff are going to have on the textile industry in his riding. As to the hon. member for Rosetown, his remarks were of a general character, and showed that he is too blameless and pure and high-principled to be able to contribute anything of practical value to an economic discussion of this kind. I think we all agree with many of the principles that he enunciates, but I am afraid that in this practical age the hon. member will find himself like a solitary sparrow on a housetop or a lonely pelican in the wilderness.
Now. sir, coming from the constituency in which is situated the great steel industry of eastern Canada, I have to express my regret that the budget holds out no hope for that industry. Two years ago the Duncan report made certain recommendations with regard to it. One year ago the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) gave a message of hope to the people of the maritime provinces when he stated that the government intended to implement fully those recommendations. Two years ago the industry submitted its case to the tariff board, asking for more protection, but so far as I am aware nothing has yet been heard from the board. One year ago the Prime Minister gave as a reason for not taking immediate action to implement the Duncan report with respect to the steel industry that the British Empire Steel Corporation was in litigation, and he stated that nothing would be done until matters had been (straightened out. Now ithe litigation has been settled, everything has been straightened out, and all we want at this time is some indication on the part of the government, some gesture of their intention to give assistance to that industry; but none is forthcoming. We had reason to hope, and did hope up to the very time the budget was brought down, that some assistance would be given to the steel industry of Nova Scotia.
I have no desire to embarrass the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot). In a speech delivered at St. John a short time before Christmas he intimated that when the budget was brought down, or at some very near time in the future, the two major recommendations of the Duncan report, one with regard to the Valley railway and the other with regard to the steel industry, would receive attention, and the news in relation to these matters would be such as to make every maritimer glad. Well, the speech was delivered at a convivial assembly by a minister speaking to his constituents; he would naturally have a strong desire to give them a word of hope and encouragement, and it was to be expected that he would speak in that vein; but I for one refuse to believe that his statement was entirely unwarranted. I believe that at the time the government did intend to do something for our steel industry. What has happened in the meantime to cause them to change their minds? Has anything happened, or are they going to postpone action for another year in order to be able to make political capital out of any concession then granted to the industry?
I am not going to take up any time discussing the question of debt and taxation, for it has already been fairly well threshed out, and I think it is pretty well understood by the people of Canada. I do not understand the great jubilation with which the government's announcement of a surplus is greeted. Unless the government can prove that they themselves have done something to earn that surplus by some legislative or administrative action, I do not see any occasion for such jubilation. At the time of confederation the province of Nova Scotia handed over all her revenues to the Dominion. To-day we are having a hard struggle down there to make both ends meet. In other words, the provincial authorities are finding it very difficult to raise sufficient money to carry on the government of the province. Contrast that lack of revenue with the federal surpluses running from forty million dollars to seventy million dollars. It seems to me that the lesson to be drawn from this disparity between the financial condition of Nova Scotia and that of the Dominion is that the time has now arrived for a considered adjustment of the financial arrangement between the provincial and the federal authorities. The federal government has from time to time invaded the field of provincial taxation, crippling the various provincial administrations, and to-day most of the provinces are experiencing considerable difficulty in meet-
742	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. MacDonald (Cape Breton)
ing their budget requirements. Even in the small matter of the fines that come in from prosecutions under the customs and excise act, although the provincial government furnishes all the officers and provides gaol accommodation when the prisoners are convicted, the fines go into the federal exchequer. The provincial government has to bear all the expenses. I think in fairness this government should refund to the province and to the various municipalities all the fines that have been collected from prosecutions under the act.
There is another matter closely associated with this question of the relation between the municipalities and the provincial governments on the one hand and the federal government on the other. The country store is passing away; the small storekeepers in the various towns and rural districts are going out of business. These people are being gradually driven out by the mail order houses. In my home city of Sydney I have seen a large room in the post office filled with mail bags crammed with catalogues from mail order houses. The people from the various rural districts send their money to these houses and get goods in return. This practice may possibly be defended on the ground that the goods are cheaper. Very well. But I ask in all seriousness why this government should use the post office department to facilitate the carrying on of this business without making some recompense to the municipality that is being hurt. The local storekeeper has to pay a certain amount of taxation for the upkeep of the town; the mail order house pays nothing. I submit that the time has come when these mail order houses should be made to pay a share of the taxation in the municipalities that are being affected, so that the local storekeeper may be given a chance for his life.
This forty minute rule, Mr. Speaker, is pretty much the same as a three months' note which a man has to meet: the time goes very rapidly. I have not an opportunity to develop any one of the questions which I should like to discuss, but I must hurry on now to the subject which is of supreme importance to me, namely, our fuel supply. We are all agreed in this country as to the great necessity of establishing some fuel policy-a national fuel policy if you will. We all admit that it is highly desirable that we should make this country independent in this respect. We have in Canada an ample supply of coal; at both ends of the country there are large coal deposits. But we are sending out of Canada over $100,000,000 a year for the purchase of coal which could be
fMr. F. MacDonald.]
supplied from our own deposits if only we were able to make them available. Of course, our difficulty lies right there. These coal deposits are to be found on either side of the country while the great consuming portion of the population is situated about midway. It seems a somewhat sad commentary on our boasted civilization that under such circumstances the miners of Canada should be in dire distress and that public subscriptions should have to be called for in order to feed and clothe them during the winter. This is going on from year to year and nothing practical appears to be suggested. Surely something can be done and ought to be done to meet the situation. Our problem in the province of Nova Scotia is winter unemployment. During the summer months we are able to ship our coal to the St. Lawrence market, but for four months in the winter our mines are practically idle and our miners out of employment. Some sort of cure has been offered by means of the banking of coal in winter. This in my opinion is a very poor substitute, because after all the banking of coal in winter simply takes that amount of the market away in the summer time. There should be some more satisfactory way of solving this problem of winter unemployment.
During the past three years we have had a number of investigations into the coal question and various suggestions have been offered. The witnesses who have appeared before the committees all express a desire for a national fuel policy, but no one will tell us what that policy should be. I do not intend to propose what I believe to be a national fuel policy, but I do wish to submit to this government some constructive suggestions which I trust will have some effect in alleviating the circumstances of winter unemployment in Nova Scotia. Let me state the problem simply to the house. It costs us $3.80 a ton for coal at the pit mouth and another $3.80 to land it in Montreal; that is $7.60. American coal can be laid down there $2 cheaper than this figure. How shall we meet the competition? I confess that when I came to this parliament two or three years ago I had the idea that the whole question could very easily be solved; all that was necessary was a high tariff against coal coming in from the American mines in such large quantities. I have learned since that the tariff is only one factor in a very complex problem, and that if we are to cope with the question of unemployment in Nova Scotia there are three or four factors that have to be considered and three or four parties to the problem who will have to make sacrifices.

The Budget-Mr. Bourgeois
We have to meet American coal in the St. Lawrence valley, and to do so we must either cut our costs somewhat, or raise American costs to some extent, or do a little of both. I want to submit the suggestion to the government that it is possible to attain this end by a little sacrifice on the part of everyone. The operator must make some sacrifice and produce his coaJl at a rate lower than $3.30; the traffic man must make a sacrifice and transport his coal from Sydney to Montreal at a rate lower than $3.80, and the local government must make some sacrifice by refunding a portion, if not all, of the tax on the coal mined during the four winter months, because this is the particular time to which I am referring.
How are we going to do that? The idea is suggested by this famous Duncan report. Before the Duncan commission was appointed the maritime provinces were more or less in the doldrums; they were discouraged and rather hopeless; men were leaving and the industries were failing. The Duncan commission held sittings and brought in certain recommendations which, although they have not all been carried out, were still very hopeful, and the statement of the Prime Minister that it was the intention of his government to implement those recommendations had a wonderful effect throughout the maritime provinces. Now, the idea is this: Can we not have a commission similar to the Duncan commission to deal with this problem of winter unemployment in Nova Scotia? Let me make this suggestion to the government: Appoint a commission of five men, one representing the companies, one representing the traffic department of the great railway, one representing the industry, one leading business man and last but not least a representative of the miners of Nova Scotia, and let me say that the miners will send to that conference a man with an intelligence equal to that of any other man there present, and probably with a greater knowledge of the actual condition of affairs. There is no need to take any evidence; the evidence is all here and the facts are all in the possession of the Department of Mines. I am sorry the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is not here to-night, or I would try to secure from him an assurance of his willingness to consider the idea. Possibly the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) may give me his assurance. I venture to think that if such a conference as this is held a solution will be found, and a recommendation from that commission will be of sufficient weight, backed up by public sentiment, to effect a remedy for this great unemployment. This is not a cure-all; I am not offering this as a fuel policy but rather as a pure experiment to deal with this question in a practical way. Up to the present no person on either side of the house and no witness whom I have heard or of. whom I have read has ventured to make any practical suggestion which would offer a solution of this difficulty.	*
This is an important and vital question to the maritime provinces. Every year we have a recurrence of these same distressing conditions; every year our miners and their wives and children are in dire distress and have to be helped with food, clothing and the other necessities of life. Surely the time has come in the history of this country when there is sufficient intelligence and patriotism on the part of the general public to make some sacrifice, not only to alleviate the sufferings of these men but that out of it may possibly grow something which will furnish a permanent solution of this very difficult problem.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a feeling of hesitancy that I rise on this occasion, because I readily understand that it is the duty of a member attempting to address this house for the first time to move cautiously; for there is always that danger of wandering too far afield and of having to be reminded to tread the straight and narrow path. For that reason, Sir, I will be brief in my remarks.
It is my first duty on the occasion of this, my first address in this house, to extend to you, Sir, my congratulations on your unanimous selection for the third time to the exalted position of Speaker of this house. This is unquestionable and conclusive proof of your nation wide known impartiality and of your unfailing courtesy and distinctive personality. Although most of the people of our province, so far as I am aware, have never had the honour of your personal acquaintance, I can assure you that your distinguished career in the service of our country is a household topic in the province of New Brunswick, and particularly in the constituency which I have the honour to represent. May I also say that we admire the province of Quebec for the number of talented and distinguished statesmen it has contributed to the public service of Canada.
It is also my desire to congratulate the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) on his elevation to the position he now occupies at the head of the great Conservative party. I am particularly pleased at this because of the
The Budget-Mr. Bourgeois

fact that he comes from the province of New Brunswick and was born in the county of Albert, which is adjacent to my own county. I am confident that in time, if it is his ultimate destiny to become Prime Minister of this great Dominion, he will uphold the best traditions of our New Brunswick statesmen who have sat in the councils of the nation, and will bring to that exalted position those high ideals of the true Canadian statesman which he possesses in full measure.
It is also my pleasure to congratulate the mover (Mr. Ilsley) and the seconder (Mr. Beaubien) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne for the very masterly manner in which they performed their part. I can assure them that they have won not only the admiration of their constituents but also the respect of this house and of the entire country.
Unquestionably the outstanding event of every session of parliament is the presentation of the budget by the Minister of Finance. Although I was not a member of this house until 1926, nevertheless I have followed the trend of events very closely, and I am sure that the great majority of the hon. members of this house will agree with me when I say that at every successive budget presentation the people of Canada as well as the unbiased press of our country have been loud in their praise of the administration of the public affairs of Canada by the present government and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) whose reputation as an honest, sound and economic administrator of the finances of Canada ranks high in the minds of the people. I believe that our expectations of sound economic progress throughout Canada have been again demonstrated by the minister in his presentation of the budget this year.
It is not my purpose, Mr. Speaker, to review what has taken place in Canada since the 14th of September, 1926, for many of the speakers on this side of the house dealt very ably with the conditions at that time when the speech from the throne was discussed. But, Sir, I must say that on that date the, electorate of Canada responded nobly to the appeal to elect a stable government, a government with a truly national policy and one only for every section of Canada. Embodied in that policy are the three essentials of a moderate tariff policy, a policy of adequate protection for the manufacturers of Canada, and one of wider markets for every section and class of industry throughout our country. Do we need, Sir, any greater proof of the wisdom of this policy than the changed conditions brought about since 1921? Year after year 
we are witnessing a gradual reduction of our national debt. Year after year we are also witnessing a large favourable trade balance, and we are pleased to note this year an excess of exports over imports amounting to the large sum of $147,100,904, due, Mr. Speaker, not only to the wise policy of the government, but also to the indefatigable energies and cooperation of the agricultural and industrial population in every province of Canada. But special mention should be made of the agricultural population of the western provinces in contributing in such a large measure towards this favourable trade balance, and I desire to say, Sir, that the pioneers and their families who went west from the provinces of Ontario and Quebec and from the provinces down by the sea, and the folks who emigrated from the British Isles and other lands to western Canada, deserve the greatest commendation for their courage and perseverance in carving out of the Northwest territories the beautiful provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. They have accomplished the great achievement of making of western Canada the greatest wheat producing country in the world, and have thereby also contributed to a great extent to the success of the two great railway systems of Canada.
But one must not forget that Ontario, the banner province of Canada, has been a great factor in increasing our favourable trade balance, due to the highly industrialized conditions in that province and its intensive agricultural production. Another contributing factor has been the province of Quebec with its immense resources of forest wealth of wood pulp products and its sane economic hydro development policy, which have had the effect of attracting an enormous amount of foreign capital to that province.
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that in New Brunswick our progress has not been as marked along agricultural and industrial lines as that of the central and western provinces. That is due to some extent to our geographical situation and to our remoteness from the markets of the central provinces; also to the almost prohibitive tariff which prevents us from placing our surplus agricultural products in the markets of the United States, particularly potatoes, of which we have a large surplus every year and on which there is a duty of 50 cents per 100 pounds. Not only does that tariff adversely affect our agricultural population, but it also prejudicially affects our fishing industry to the extent of two cents per pound on mackerel, two cents on halibut and one cent on cod. It is therefore of the utmost importance to the maritime provinces that the government should undertake negotiations at

the earliest opportunity whereby our products of the soil, the forest and the sea may be admitted to the United States market under most favourable conditions.
But Sir, notwithstanding the disadvantages in that direction a spirit of optimism prevails throughout the province of New Brunswick, and a feeling of the greatest confidence in the future. This spirit has been stimulated by the fostering influence of the government in the opening of wider markets and by the negotiations of the British West Indies treaty; and with the prospects of a greater expansion of trade with the Central and South American republics the agricultural population are bending their energies to a more intensive agricultural production. As a proof of that assertion I may say that the estimated value of our field crop production in 1927 was $23,596,000. Of potatoes alone we had under cultivation 46,998 acres yielding to the farmers of New Brunswick at a conservative estimate a return of $5,423,000. Not only are they directing their energies towards a greater agricultural production but they are also paying attention to the dairy industry. In 1925 our dairy production amounted to $7,663,174. In 1926 it amounted to $8,046,743, a production which is still insufficient to meet the requirements of the home consumption of the province, particularly in butter. If the same increase is kept up from year to year we shall very soon, I hope, have a surplus. Until then the agriculturists of New Brunswick will have no cause to complain of the effects of the Australian treaty in so far as its results upon the butter market are concerned.
Coming to the fishing industry of the province of New Brunswisk, I must say that it is of the greatest importance to a large population located in the area extending from Camp-bellton on the Baie des Chaleurs to Cape Tormentine on the southernmost extremity of New Brunswick on Northumberland strait, an industry from which the fishermen benefited to the extent of $2,375,000 in 1926, and $2,520,722 in 1927. May I point out that the county of Kent occupies a very prominent position in that regard, particularly in- the catch of lobsters and oysters. Within my constituency we have two lobster fishing seasons, one applicable to the district extending from Point Sapin on the north to Chock-fish on the south, which opens on April 26th and closes on June 26th, and the other applicable to the district from Chockfish to River Philip in the county of Cumberland, Nova Scotia, opening on August 15th and closing on October 15th. Between the two last mentioned points there is unquestionably
great dissatisfaction among the fishermen due to the lateness of the opening date. I would point out to hon. members that owing td the prevailing high winds and frequent and sometimes very violent and disastrous storms, the fishermen are unable to overhaul their lobster traps, and as a consequence can avail themselves of but three weeks out of a period of two months. The result has been that a great many have abandoned their occupation. I therefore hope that the royal fisheries commission in their investigations will have found conditions such as to justify the recommendation that the lobster season instead of beginning on August 15th and ending on October 15th, begin the first of August and end the 30th September. I would further particularly recommend that in order that our fishermen may be protected in their at all times hazardous and dangerous occupation in the open seas of Northumberland strait, where frequent storms arise which are sometimes very disastrous to life and property, more protection be afforded along our coast. In this connection, I would point out to the Minister of Public Works ('Mr. Elliott) that in the county oi Kent breakwaters are absolutely essential at St. Louis, Maillet's gully and Caissie cape for the protection of our fishermen along that part of the coast.
As regards the Duncan report, we are particularly grateful to the government for implementing the recommendations contained therein, especially the twenty per cent reduction in freight rates, a reduction which is and will be of incalculable benefit to the agricultural, commercial and industrial life of the maritime provinces. In regard to the recommendation with respect to railway matters in Kent, I hope the government will at an early day so adjust matters as to relieve the unsatisfactory conditions which have existed in the northern part for many years.
Another recommendation of the Duncan report, which is implemented and for which the fishing population are very grateful, is the appointment of the royal fisheries commission to inquire into fishing conditions in the maritime provinces. Its report when submitted will, I hope, tend in a large measure towards remedying the grievances of the fishermen and also towards, a greater development of that very important industry in the maritime provinces.
In conclusion, it is my pleasure to say that we have in New Brunswick a strong and virile population characteristic of the two great English and French-speaking races, living in the most perfect harmony and

mutual good fellowship, and conscious of their duty to assist in making Canada a happy, prosperous and united country.
